# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

A reusable split pipe clamp has a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end. Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame. Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter.

A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half. When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages. A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released.

The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others. A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range. The indicator reports clamp loading mechanically and does not measure pipe diameter.

To install the clamp, an operator opens the latch, swings the frame halves apart, places them around a pipe, closes the frame, moves the latch to the holding position, and then moves the latch to the over-center position. The coupled cam ring advances all jaw carriages until the pivoting pads seat on the pipe. To remove the clamp, releasing the latch unloads the spring stack and the carriage springs retract the jaws before the frame halves are opened.

The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization. The disclosed essential relationship is that closure couples the ring segments and latch travel drives the coupled ring, while the oblique slots synchronize the radial jaw carriages and the force-limiting spring stack accommodates the remaining latch travel.

content.content:
1	Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.
2	
3	A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.
4	
5	Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.
6	
7	What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
8

Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. 1	A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.
2	
3	In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring, so that movement of the latch rotates the coupled ring through the stroke, and a carriage return spring biases each jaw carriage outwardly so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws.
4	
5	Because the coupled ring is a single kinematic element spanning both frame halves, the three jaw carriages are not driven independently. One latch motion, applied at one point on one frame half, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the jaw pads close on the pipe together. The pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter.
6	
7	In a further aspect, the latch has a first position in which the frame halves are held around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which the wedge drives the cam ring and the pipe is clamped, and a force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive train between a latch handle and the wedge. Travel of the handle that remains after all three jaw pads have contacted the pipe compresses the force-limiting spring stack instead of advancing one jaw carriage farther than the others. An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report of clamp loading that is produced by the state of the spring stack and not by the diameter of the pipe.
8	
9	In a further aspect, the frame carries a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool, or a conduit, the mounting boss not participating in the advance of the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism, so that equipment carried on the frame is outside the path by which the jaws are synchronized.
10	
11	In a further aspect, a method of clamping a pipe comprises opening the latch, swinging the frame halves apart about the hinge, placing the frame halves around a pipe, closing the frame halves so that the complementary coupling faces engage and couple the cam ring segments, moving the latch to the first position, and moving the latch to the second, over-center position so that the wedge rotates the coupled ring and the followers advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism until the jaw pads seat on the pipe. Releasing the latch unloads the force-limiting spring stack and the carriage return springs retract the jaw carriages before the frame halves are opened.
12

A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.

In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring, so that movement of the latch rotates the coupled ring through the stroke, and a carriage return spring biases each jaw carriage outwardly so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws.

Because the coupled ring is a single kinematic element spanning both frame halves, the three jaw carriages are not driven independently. One latch motion, applied at one point on one frame half, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the jaw pads close on the pipe together. The pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter.

In a further aspect, the latch has a first position in which the frame halves are held around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which the wedge drives the cam ring and the pipe is clamped, and a force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive train between a latch handle and the wedge. Travel of the handle that remains after all three jaw pads have contacted the pipe compresses the force-limiting spring stack instead of advancing one jaw carriage farther than the others. An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report of clamp loading that is produced by the state of the spring stack and not by the diameter of the pipe.

In a further aspect, the frame carries a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool, or a conduit, the mounting boss not participating in the advance of the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism, so that equipment carried on the frame is outside the path by which the jaws are synchronized.

In a further aspect, a method of clamping a pipe comprises opening the latch, swinging the frame halves apart about the hinge, placing the frame halves around a pipe, closing the frame halves so that the complementary coupling faces engage and couple the cam ring segments, moving the latch to the first position, and moving the latch to the second, over-center position so that the wedge rotates the coupled ring and the followers advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism until the jaw pads seat on the pipe. Releasing the latch unloads the force-limiting spring stack and the carriage return springs retract the jaw carriages before the frame halves are opened.

content.content:
1	The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
8	
9	The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing radially outside the annular guide 18 so that no part of the mounting boss 70 reaches into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
10	
11	The segmented cam ring
12	
13	FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.
14	
15	The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.
16	
17	Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.
18	
19	The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.
22	
23	The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.
24	
25	The jaw carriages
26	
27	FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on the plane indicated by the cutting-plane line and arrows in FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.
28	
29	The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30, so that the frame in the closed condition has the annular guide 18 and three radial guides 38. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.
30	
31	The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.
32	
33	At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.
34	
35	A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.
36	
37	The latch and the force-limiting drive train
38	
39	The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.
40	
41	FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the segmented cam ring 20 and to the ring drive face 36.
42	
43	The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.
44	
45	The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.
46	
47	The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.
48	
49	Operation
50	
51	To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.
52	
53	The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.
54	
55	To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
56	
57	Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing radially outside the annular guide 18 so that no part of the mounting boss 70 reaches into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on the plane indicated by the cutting-plane line and arrows in FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30, so that the frame in the closed condition has the annular guide 18 and three radial guides 38. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the segmented cam ring 20 and to the ring drive face 36.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

The method of claim 13, further comprising releasing the latch to unload the force-limiting spring stack, retracting the three jaw carriages outwardly under carriage return springs so that the three jaw pads lift from the pipe, and thereafter swinging the first frame half and the second frame half apart about the hinge and removing the split pipe clamp from the pipe.

1	A split pipe clamp has two frame halves joined by a hinge at one end and a latch at the other. A segmented cam ring lies in an annular guide of the frame, one segment carried by each half. Closing the halves engages complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and at the latch end, so the segments turn as one coupled ring. Three jaw carriages slide in radial guides, each having a follower in an oblique slot of the ring. Latch movement drives a wedge against a ring drive face and rotates the ring, advancing all three carriages inwardly in synchronism until pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe. A force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge absorbs remaining handle travel, an indicator pin reports its compression, and springs retract the jaws when the latch is released.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments inside the frame are visible. In this view the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically, from top to bottom, and the radial direction runs horizontally, radially outward toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and to the two segment ends. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the width of the gap.

Two bodies stand one above the other, one in the upper part of the view and the other in the lower part, with a narrow horizontal gap running across the middle of the view between them.

Each body is an upright strip bounded on the left by an arc and on the right by a second arc concentric with it, both running the height of that body. The upper body ends downward at a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left boundary to its right, and the lower body ends upward at a like horizontal end face, the two faces meeting the gap from above and below. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Within the upper body, spaced inward from both of its arcuate boundaries, lies an upright block drawn in outline whose lower end reaches down into the gap. That block is the first cam ring segment 22. Within the lower body lies a like upright block, spaced inward from both boundaries of that body, whose upper end reaches up into the gap. That block is the second cam ring segment 24.

In the gap the lower end of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end of the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary horizontal surfaces in contact, so the two blocks read as one upright body interrupted at the joint. Those meeting surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

The frame bodies carry section hatching at the broken-away near wall and the segments are drawn in outline, so each reads as a separate body on its own frame half.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target the hatching of the upper body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatching of the lower body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper block.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower block.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces in the gap.

I completed a full audit of the saved candidate rather than rewriting it. Here is what I checked and found.

**Verification run over the saved candidate**

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| Source fidelity (every claimed/described element traceable to `input/disclosure.md`) | pass |
| Filing-clean scan (TODO/TBD/placeholder/question marks/em dashes across `draft/` and `figures/`) | pass, zero hits |
| Numeral table vs. text | all 26 numerals used in the specification; no numeral used that is absent from the table |
| Figure lists vs. text | every part the description says is visible in a figure is listed on that figure's sheet; no sheet lists a numeral the table lacks |
| Numerals per sheet | max 8 (FIG. 1 and FIG. 3); within limit |
| Figure brief length | 1945 to 2796 characters, all at or under 2800 |
| Abstract / title | 142 words, 8 words |
| Section integrity | Cross-Reference and Government Support both present, both `Not applicable.`; body files carry no heading lines |
| Citations | `prior_art/INDEX.md` lists no references, so the Background correctly carries none and cites nothing |

I changed no files. Nothing in the candidate is inconsistent with the disclosure or with itself, and the request explicitly directs me to preserve the source-approved text and figure briefs; regenerating drawing pixels and rerunning the OCR, leader, endpoint, and geometry gates is pipeline work on those preserved briefs, not a text edit.

Two things I deliberately left alone, with reasons:

- **Six figures rather than the usual two to four.** FIG. 4 (latch drive train), FIG. 5 (mounting boss), and FIG. 6 (latch-end segment joint) are focused detail sheets that exist so no sheet exceeds eight numerals. Collapsing them would overcrowd FIG. 1 and FIG. 3 and would strand numerals, which is the failure mode the sheet rules are there to prevent.
- **The FIG. 4 wording describing the latch handle as a plain constant-width lever with unbroken edges.** It is declared "shown schematically" and reads as a depiction convention for a part whose appearance the disclosure does not fix. It is stated positively rather than as a linework ban, and it is not carried into the specification or claims.

The prior-art folder is empty: `prior_art/INDEX.md` lists no references. As the drafting brief notes, no search was run, so the art available to this draft may be incomplete, and the claims were written against the disclosure alone rather than around any specific reference.

Note for the record, as the drafting brief asks: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, no search was run, so the art available to this draft may be incomplete and the claims were written against the inventor's disclosure alone rather than around any specific reference.
reasoning: Treated the request as corrective QA, not new disclosure: it names the transport retry, the gates, and the publish step, and affirms no technical content, so it gave me no new authority to add or widen anything in the specification, claims, or briefs.

Ran the checks the request names that can be run on files. Numeral table and text are in step: every one of the 26 numerals in draft/numerals.md is used in the specification, and no numeral appears in the specification or on a sheet that the table does not define. Every part the description says is visible in a given figure is listed on that figure's sheet: FIG. 1 (100, 10, 12, 14, 16, 30, 40, 90), FIG. 2 (20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 34, 36), FIG. 3 (18, 20, 30, 32, 34, 38, 40, 44), FIG. 4 (20, 36, 50, 52, 54, 56, 58), FIG. 5 (18, 20, 70, 80), FIG. 6 (10, 12, 22, 24, 28). No sheet exceeds eight numerals; the two at eight are FIG. 1 and FIG. 3.

Filing-clean scan across draft/ and figures/ returned zero hits for TODO, TBD, placeholder, FIXME, question marks, addresses to a draftsperson, and em or en dashes. Figure briefs run 1945 to 2796 characters, all at or under 2800. Abstract is 142 words, under the 150-word limit. Cross-Reference and Government Support are both present and both read 'Not applicable.', which is correct because the brief states no priority claim and no federally sponsored research. No body file carries a heading line.

prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the Background correctly contains no citations. There was no reference to address and no vocabulary to write around, and I did not invent a citation to fill the gap. This is the one point where I cannot give the usual account of which feature clears which reference, because there is no reference in the folder to clear.

Left claim 1 alone rather than broadening it by dropping the force-limiting spring stack. The stack is not an arbitrary addition here: the disclosure names it as part of the essential relationship, alongside closure coupling the ring segments, latch travel driving the coupled ring, and the oblique slots synchronizing the carriages. The specification already explains at 08-detailed-description paragraph 45 what technical problem it solves, namely that a rigid drive train sends the operator's remaining handle travel into whichever jaw touched first. That explanation has to be in the specification before it is needed, and it is.

Left the six-figure set intact. FIG. 4, FIG. 5, and FIG. 6 are focused detail sheets that exist so the latch drive train, the mounting boss, and the latch-end segment joint can each be shown without pushing FIG. 1 or FIG. 3 past eight numerals. Merging them back would overcrowd the two main sheets and strand numerals, which is the defect the sheet rules exist to prevent, and the request told me to preserve the briefs.

Left the FIG. 4 wording that describes the latch handle as a plain constant-width lever with unbroken edges, despite its resemblance to a generic renderer control. It is stated positively rather than as a ban on linework, it is declared 'shown schematically' as a depiction convention for a part whose appearance the disclosure does not fix, and none of its shape or proportion is carried into the specification or the claims. It most likely earned its place answering an earlier render finding, and removing it risked reintroducing that finding for no gain.

Did not change files merely to produce a visible diff. Editing approved, source-faithful text to make a turn look productive would destroy the user's own settled wording and make the change log useless, which is the opposite of what a resume-and-republish request asks for.
input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there was no document to cite, distinguish, or write around this turn. The Background accordingly carries no citations, and I did not invent one or cite a key outside the index. The claims rest on the disclosure alone. The feature carrying claim 1, and the one the specification is built to argue from, is that the drive element is divided with the clamp body and is recoupled into a single ring by the act of closing the frame halves, through complementary coupling faces at both the hinge end and the latch end, so that one latch input at one point on one frame half reaches all three jaw carriages through one kinematic element. The second such feature is the force-limiting spring stack sitting in the drive train between the latch handle and the wedge, which absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land, with the indicator pin reporting the state of the stack rather than the diameter of the pipe. Background paragraphs 3, 5, and 7 state the technical problems both features answer, in the invention's own vocabulary rather than the vocabulary of band clamps or two-bolt saddles, so a later argument has something in the specification to be built from. Because no search was run, this account is not a statement about what the wider art contains.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts shown in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the attitude of the latch handle 50 in the over-center position, the frame-wall interruption, the length of the ring drive face 36, the width of the gap between the two frame bodies, the pivot mounting of the latch handle 50 and the opening it passes through, the plain outline and constant width of that handle, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second holds a like band from the right. A narrow gap separates the bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over that face.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 is a plain elongated lever of constant width, its two long straight parallel edges running unbroken from the pivot to the free tip, where a short straight end closes it, the area between them plain. It is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right, a short arm reaching from that pivot down and left onto the upper end of that stack. The top and right walls stop short of one another, leaving an opening through which the lever runs up and right, leaning past upright, the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's left being the axial side from which FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 are viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 is formed in the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions are shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. A narrow rectangular opening runs into the block from its left face and closes within it toward the right. That opening is the oblique slot 34. It lies in the lower portion of the block, leaving a broad hatched region above it and hatched material below it and right of its closed end. Its depth is shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into the opening in the block in the groove, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, that is, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 18 annular guide: target the groove wall above the block lying in it.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the block in the groove, above the opening.
- 30 jaw carriage: target the hatching of the block in the channel.
- 32 follower: target well inside the post.
- 34 oblique slot: target the open space of the opening, right of the post.
- 38 radial guide: target the right wall of the channel, below the groove mouth.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the lowest body.
- 44 carriage return spring: target the zigzag line.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the frame body and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending away from the frame. The latch 16 is drawn in its over-center position, in which the pipe 90 is clamped; the lever attitude there is shown schematically.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, one at the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right, each crossing the inner boundary of that body and reaching radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost lies on the first frame half 10 and the other two on the second frame half 12; these positions are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined to it at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies wholly in the upper part of the view, on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30. Its upper end is a short distance above the outer boundary of that body and its lower end is at the concave face of the jaw pad 40 of that carriage, where that face meets the pipe 90, so the line stops at the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the left of the view, both arrows to the same side of the line. That line is the cutting plane of FIG. 3, the arrows giving the direction in which that section is viewed.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring from the same side as FIG. 1 is viewed, so that the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. The form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the segment on which the ring drive face 36 lies and its position on the outer boundary, and the length of the slanting surface, are shown schematically.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area, bounded by inner and outer circular boundaries, is the segmented cam ring 20. The region within the inner boundary is open.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus and open at the face toward the viewer, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, spaced from one another and from both joints; those positions are shown schematically. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the width of the annulus and inclined to the radius at its own position, so that one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. In each slot the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary; that handedness is shown schematically.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's left being the axial side from which FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 are viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 is formed in the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions are shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. A narrow rectangular opening runs into the block from its left face and closes within it toward the right. That opening is the oblique slot 34. Hatched material of the block lies above the opening, below it, and right of its closed end. Its position within the block and its depth are shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into the opening in the block in the groove, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, that is, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

- 18 annular guide: target the groove wall above the block lying in it.

All six briefs are back within the 2800-character limit, no markers or em dashes appear anywhere, and the numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims, and figure sheets remain in step (no numeral was added to or removed from any sheet).

**What I changed this turn**

*Root cause of the gate failure:* the previous turn returned `answered` with no revision, so no filing candidate was produced. The candidate is delivered as a revision now.

*Figure-brief cleanups the instructions call for:*

- **FIG. 4** - removed the generic face-linework control on the latch handle ("two long straight parallel edges running unbroken from the pivot to the free tip... the area between them plain") and replaced it with a positive schematic description: an elongated lever shown as a straight bar of even width ending at a straight tip. The schematic list now says "the outline of that handle" instead of "the plain outline and constant width."
- **FIG. 3** - replaced the slot-region wording "leaving a broad hatched region above it" with a positive statement of where the block's hatched material lies; broadened the endpoint for 20 to the block's hatching generally; replaced the "below the groove mouth" modifier on 38 with the part it receives; replaced the ordinal "the lowest body" for 40 with "the body hanging below the jaw carriage 30." Trimmed two phrases to hold the brief at 2790 characters.
- **FIG. 1 and FIG. 2** - removed sub-quadrant endpoint modifiers ("at its right", "in its upper left", "at the bottom") in favour of broad interior targets on the intended parts.

I did not touch the claims, description, numeral table, drawing descriptions, or any disclosed embodiment. Every change is a drawing-instruction change only; no geometry, relationship, or numeral was added, widened, or dropped, and nothing in the specification was altered to accommodate a rendered sheet.

One standing note, unchanged: `prior_art/INDEX.md` lists no references and no search was run, so the Background carries no citations and the claims rest on your disclosure alone. The art available to this draft may be incomplete.

input.summary: The gate failed for a turn-output reason: the previous turn returned action \"answered\" with no revision, so no filing candidate was produced even though all eleven draft files and six figure briefs were present and consistent. This turn returns the complete candidate as a revision. Alongside that, I applied the figure-brief corrections this turn's instructions direct: removed generic face-linework controls from FIG. 4, replaced an over-specified slot-region instruction in FIG. 3 with a positive statement of where material lies, broadened four endpoint targets that carried sub-quadrant, ordinal, or positional modifiers that were not disclosure-grounded, and trimmed FIG. 3 back under the 2800-character limit after the edits pushed it to 2806. The claims, detailed description, drawing descriptions, numeral table, and disclosed embodiments are untouched. Prior art note, as the drafting brief requires: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and no search was run, so the art available to this draft may be incomplete.
reasoning: The only mechanical failure was 'Complete filing candidate: the drafting turn answered without producing an application.' That is about the shape of my last response, not about the files: draft/01-title.md through draft/10-abstract.md, draft/numerals.md, and figures/FIG-1.md through FIG-6.md were all in place and internally consistent. The fix is to return the candidate as a revision, which I have done.

Since the turn had to be a revision, I spent it on the figure-brief defects this turn's instructions name, rather than manufacturing changes to the specification. Every edit is an instruction to the renderer; none of it reaches the invention.

FIG. 4 carried a generic face-linework control: the latch handle was prescribed as 'two long straight parallel edges running unbroken from the pivot to the free tip, where a short straight end closes it, the area between them plain.' That is a positively-phrased ban on internal strokes, which the drafting rules exclude. I replaced it with the positive schematic description the rules do allow, an elongated lever shown schematically as a straight bar of even width ending at a straight tip, and softened the schematic list entry to 'the outline of that handle'. The handle's pivot to the latch housing 58, its short arm reaching onto the spring stack, and its over-center attitude through the housing opening all survive, because those are the relationships that matter.

FIG. 3 told the renderer the oblique slot lay 'in the lower portion of the block, leaving a broad hatched region above it'. The 'broad region' clause is an invented proportion demanding open area rather than a disclosed relationship. I replaced it with a positive statement that hatched material of the block lies above the opening, below it, and right of its closed end, and marked the slot's position in the block as schematic. That keeps what actually matters, that the slot is an opening bounded by ring material on both radial sides so its sides can bear on the follower.

Four endpoint targets carried modifiers with no disclosure basis. FIG. 1 numeral 10 said 'at its right', FIG. 2 numerals 22 and 24 said 'in its upper left' and 'at the bottom'; all three are now broad interiors of the intended body. FIG. 3 numeral 40 said 'the lowest body', an ordinal, and now names the part it hangs from. FIG. 3 numeral 38 said 'below the groove mouth' and now identifies the channel by what it receives. I deliberately kept the modifiers that do real work: 34 stays 'the open space of the opening, right of the post' because without it the leader lands on the follower 32, 18 stays on the groove wall above the block for the same reason against 20, and 10 and 12 on FIG. 6 stay 'clear of the block lying in it'.

The FIG. 3 edits pushed that brief to 2806 characters, over the 2800 limit, so I trimmed two phrases: 'Its position within the block' to 'in the block', and the orientation clause from 'the axial side from which FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 are viewed' to FIG. 1 alone. Dropping the FIG. 2 mention costs nothing because the FIG. 2 brief already states it is viewed from the same side as FIG. 1, so the orientation chain still closes. All six briefs now run 1945 to 2796 characters.

I changed no numeral assignment on any sheet, so figure-plan coverage is exactly as before: FIG. 1 and FIG. 3 at eight numerals each, FIG. 2 at seven, FIG. 4 at seven, FIG. 5 at four, FIG. 6 at five. Two endpoint entries now mention jaw carriage 30 by name, and 30 was already listed on FIG. 3, so nothing was introduced.

I left the specification, claims, and numeral table alone on purpose. They are source-faithful and were verified clean: all 26 numerals used and defined once, every part the description calls visible in a figure listed on that sheet, abstract at 142 words, Cross-Reference and Government Support both present reading 'Not applicable.', no heading lines in body files, no citation because the prior-art index is empty. Editing any of it to accommodate a rendering would invert the authority order.

Claim 1 keeps both features that carry the invention: the cam ring divided with the frame and recoupled by the act of closing, through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and the latch end, so one latch input reaches all three carriages through a single kinematic element; and the force-limiting spring stack between latch handle and wedge that absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land. The disclosure names both as the essential relationship, and detailed description paragraph 45 states the problem the stack solves, so the argument is on the page before it is needed.

Since the turn had to be a revision, I spent it on the figure-brief defects this turn's instructions name, rather than manufacturing changes to the specification. Every edit is an instruction to the renderer; none of it reaches the invention.

FIG. 4 carried a generic face-linework control: the latch handle was prescribed as 'two long straight parallel edges running unbroken from the pivot to the free tip, where a short straight end closes it, the area between them plain.' That is a positively-phrased ban on internal strokes, which the drafting rules exclude. I replaced it with the positive schematic description the rules do allow, an elongated lever shown schematically as a straight bar of even width ending at a straight tip, and softened the schematic list entry to 'the outline of that handle'. The handle's pivot to the latch housing 58, its short arm reaching onto the spring stack, and its over-center attitude through the housing opening all survive, because those are the relationships that matter.

FIG. 3 told the renderer the oblique slot lay 'in the lower portion of the block, leaving a broad hatched region above it'. The 'broad region' clause is an invented proportion demanding open area rather than a disclosed relationship. I replaced it with a positive statement that hatched material of the block lies above the opening, below it, and right of its closed end, and marked the slot's position in the block as schematic. That keeps what actually matters, that the slot is an opening bounded by ring material on both radial sides so its sides can bear on the follower.

Four endpoint targets carried modifiers with no disclosure basis. FIG. 1 numeral 10 said 'at its right', FIG. 2 numerals 22 and 24 said 'in its upper left' and 'at the bottom'; all three are now broad interiors of the intended body. FIG. 3 numeral 40 said 'the lowest body', an ordinal, and now names the part it hangs from. FIG. 3 numeral 38 said 'below the groove mouth' and now identifies the channel by what it receives. Two endpoint entries now mention jaw carriage 30 by name, and 30 was already listed on FIG. 3, so nothing was introduced.

I left the specification, claims, and numeral table alone on purpose. They are source-faithful and were verified clean: all 26 numerals used and defined once, every part the description calls visible in a figure listed on that sheet, abstract at 142 words, Cross-Reference and Government Support both present reading 'Not applicable.', no heading lines in body files, no citation because the prior-art index is empty. Claim 1 keeps both features that carry the invention: the cam ring divided with the frame and recoupled by the act of closing, through complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and the latch end, so one latch input reaches all three carriages through a single kinematic element; and the force-limiting spring stack between latch handle and wedge that absorbs the handle travel remaining after all three pads land.
