Source ledger: every claim limitation, every numbered part, and every specific structure, relationship, result, operating condition, and variant in the description and figure briefs traces to an affirmative passage in input/disclosure.md (identical text is repeated in the single USER turn of input/conversation.md). Spot checks of the load-bearing items: "first frame half 10 and second frame half 12 ... semicircular ... joined at one end ... by a hinge 14 ... releasably joined at the other end ... by a releasable latch 16" ← "a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end"; "three jaw carriages 30 ... radial guide 38 ... jaw pad 40 ... pivotally mounted ... concave bearing face" ← "Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame. Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad ... without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter"; "segmented cam ring 20 ... annular guide 18 ... first cam ring segment 22 ... second cam ring segment 24 ... complementary coupling faces 26/28 ... rotate together ... as a coupled ring" ← "A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half. When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring"; "follower 32 ... oblique slot 34 ... advance ... inwardly in synchronism" and "wedge 52 ... ring drive face 36 ... stroke" ← "Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot ... Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages"; "carriage return spring 44" ← "A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released"; latch first/over-center positions, "force-limiting spring stack 54", "indicator pin 56 ... fixed edge of the latch housing 58 ... predetermined compression range ... not a measurement of that diameter", the install/remove method of claims 13-15, and "mounting boss 70 ... sensor, a tool, or a conduit ... not participating in the advance" each map to the corresponding sentences of paragraphs 9, 11 and 13 of the disclosure. Claims 1-15 add no limitation beyond that ledger; claim 10's assembly (clamp + boss + equipment) rests on "The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit." Background prior-art characterizations were not traced to the inventor, per instruction. Formalities match input/brief.md: title as given, no priority claim, no federally sponsored research, applicant/inventor Nimo Rotem.

Internal consistency: reference numerals 10-100 each carry exactly one meaning across numerals.md, the description, the claims and the figure briefs; no numeral appears in the text that is absent from the table, and every tabled numeral appears in at least one figure brief. Claim and description terminology agree ("coupled ring", "ring drive face", "force-limiting spring stack", "advance ... inwardly in synchronism"). The figure geometry is mutually consistent: FIG. 1's cutting-plane arrows put the FIG. 1 viewing side at the left of FIG. 3, which agrees with FIG. 2's slots opening toward the viewer; FIG. 4's reversed viewpoint correctly puts the second cam ring segment 24 (which carries the ring drive face 36 in FIG. 2) on the left, and the ramp handedness in FIG. 2, the drive direction in FIG. 4, and the slot handedness together produce inward jaw travel rather than retraction; FIG. 6's upper/lower assignment of frame halves matches FIG. 1. Renderer-choice items (hinge and latch outlines, carriage positions, pad and handle pivots, joint-face form, boss and equipment outlines, slot depth, guide opening direction) are hedged as "shown schematically" inside the figure briefs only; no "by way of example" or "any closed outline" broadening appears in the application text. No drafting note, placeholder, open question, unresolved alternative or internal comment remains in any file.

Two minor items only, both confined to figure briefs and drawing-reference wording: (1) the FIG. 3 section is indicated in FIG. 1 by a cutting-plane line and arrows with no view-number designation at its ends, contrary to the practice of 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3); (2) FIG. 4 asserts the direction of wedge travel ("downward movement drives the band left") without that choice being included in the brief's own schematic-depiction list, while the source is silent on the direction in which the wedge advances. Neither affects the claims, which remain neutral on both points.

## Mechanical checks that did not pass

- **Source fidelity is clean before rendering** (fail): Source ledger: every claim limitation, every numbered part, and every specific structure, relationship, result, operating condition, and variant in the description and figure briefs traces to an affirmative passage in input/disclosure.md (identical text is repeated in the single USER turn of input/conversation.md). Spot checks of the load-bearing items: "first frame half 10 and second frame half 12 ... semicircular ... joined at one end ... by a hinge 14 ... releasably joined at the other end ... by a releasable latch 16" ← "a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end"; "three jaw carriages 30 ... radial guide 38 ... jaw pad 40 ... pivotally mounted ... concave bearing face" ← "Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame. Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad ... without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter"; "segmented cam ring 20 ... annular guide 18 ... first cam ring segment 22 ... second cam ring segment 24 ... complementary coupling faces 26/28 ... rotate together ... as a coupled ring" ← "A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half. When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring"; "follower 32 ... oblique slot 34 ... advance ... inwardly in synchronism" and "wedge 52 ... ring drive face 36 ... stroke" ← "Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot ... Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages"; "carriage return spring 44" ← "A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released"; latch first/over-center positions, "force-limiting spr
  - FIG. 3 section is indicated without the view-number designation on the cutting-plane line
  - FIG. 4 brief fixes the direction of wedge advance without including that choice in its schematic-depiction list

## Reviewer findings

- **[minor] FIG. 3 section is indicated without the view-number designation on the cutting-plane line** (figures/FIG-1.md line 19; draft/07-drawings.md line 5; draft/08-detailed-description.md paragraph beginning "FIG. 3 is a) - The cutting-plane line specified in the FIG. 1 brief carries direction arrows but no Arabic numeral at its ends identifying the sectional view, and the Brief Description and the detailed description both work around the missing designation by referring to "the plane indicated by the cutting-plane line and arrows in FIG. 1" instead of the conventional "line 3-3". 37 CFR 1.84(h)(3) contemplates that the ends of the broken line be designated by numerals corresponding to the view number of the sectional view. This is a drawing-formalities gap only; the section plane itself is fully described and is consistent between FIG. 1 and FIG. 3.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-1.md, after the sentence describing the arrows, add: "The numeral 3 appears as drawing text at each end of the cutting-plane line, placed just outside that end alongside the arrow and clear of the frame body, the jaw pad 40 and the pipe 90." In draft/07-drawings.md line 5, replace "taken on the plane indicated by the cutting-plane line and arrows in FIG. 1, which plane contains" with "taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1, which plane contains". In draft/08-detailed-description.md, replace "taken on the plane indicated by the cutting-plane line and arrows in FIG. 1." with "taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1."
- **[minor] FIG. 4 brief fixes the direction of wedge advance without including that choice in its schematic-depiction list** (figures/FIG-4.md line 3 (schematic list) and line 11 ("so downward movement drives the band left")) - The FIG. 4 brief states that the wedge 52 advances radially inward (downward in the view) and thereby drives the cam ring circumferentially to the left. The disclosure says only that the latch "drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke"; it never states the direction in which the wedge advances, and the FIG. 2 brief already treats the related choice - that the ring drive face lies on the outer boundary - as schematic. The direction of wedge travel is a kinematic relationship, so it must be carried as a depiction convention rather than as an assertion of disclosed structure. The brief's own schematic list omits it, while listing the housing form, handle attitude, handle outline, pivot mounting, frame-wall interruption, drive-face length, gap width and spring-stack symbol. The application text is already neutral on this point ("The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20"), so the fix is confined to the figure brief.
  - Suggested fix: In figures/FIG-4.md line 3, extend the schematic list to read: "... the outline of that handle, the direction in which the wedge 52 advances against the ring drive face 36 and the resulting sense of movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol." Leave line 11 and all application text unchanged.

Fix every listed item before returning. If an advisory is a false positive, make
the wording or figure specification unambiguous enough that the check passes.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane corresponding to the plane of FIG. 3. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing radially outside the annular guide 18 so that no part of the mounting boss 70 reaches into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on the plane indicated by the cutting-plane line and arrows in FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30, so that the frame in the closed condition has the annular guide 18 and three radial guides 38. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the segmented cam ring 20 and to the ring drive face 36.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the frame body and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending away from the frame. The latch 16 is drawn in its over-center position, in which the pipe 90 is clamped; the lever attitude there is shown schematically.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, one at the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right, each crossing the inner boundary of that body and reaching radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost lies on the first frame half 10 and the other two on the second frame half 12; these positions are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined to it at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies wholly in the upper part of the view, on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30. Its upper end is a short distance above the outer boundary of that body and its lower end is at the concave face of the jaw pad 40 of that carriage, where that face meets the pipe 90, so the line stops at the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the left of the view, both arrows to the same side of the line. That line is the cutting plane of FIG. 3, the arrows giving the direction in which that section is viewed.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer boundary of the frame body at its upper right.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the block of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the topmost carriage inner end.
- 90 pipe: target well inside the central circle.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts shown in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the attitude of the latch handle 50 in the over-center position, the frame-wall interruption, the length of the ring drive face 36, the width of the gap between the two frame bodies, the pivot mounting of the latch handle 50 and the opening it passes through, the outline of that handle, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second holds a like band from the right. A narrow gap separates the bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over that face.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 is an elongated lever, shown schematically as a straight bar of even width ending at a straight tip. It is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right, a short arm reaching from that pivot down and left onto the upper end of that stack. The top and right walls stop short of one another, leaving an opening through which the lever runs up and right, leaning past upright, the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.

- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts shown in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the attitude of the latch handle 50 in the over-center position, the frame-wall interruption, the length of the ring drive face 36, the width of the gap between the two frame bodies, the pivot mounting of the latch handle 50 and the opening it passes through, the outline of that handle, the direction in which the wedge 52 advances against the ring drive face 36 and the resulting sense of movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second holds a like band from the right. A narrow gap separates the bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over that face.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 is an elongated lever, shown schematically as a straight bar of even width ending at a straight tip. It is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right, a short arm reaching from that pivot down and left onto the upper end of that stack. The top and right walls stop short of one another, leaving an opening through which the lever runs up and right, leaning past upright, the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

Both findings are fixed, and all six briefs are back within the 2800-character limit.

**FIG. 3 section designation (37 CFR 1.84(h)(3))**
- `figures/FIG-1.md`: the cutting-plane line now carries the view-number designation at each end, the numeral 3 set just outside the end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3. I added that it is not a reference numeral, so it cannot be mistaken for a numeral missing from `draft/numerals.md`.
- `draft/07-drawings.md` and `draft/08-detailed-description.md`: both now say "taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1" instead of the workaround wording.

**FIG. 4 wedge-advance direction**
- `figures/FIG-4.md`: the schematic-depiction list now covers "the direction in which the wedge 52 advances against the ring drive face 36 and the resulting sense of movement of the segmented cam ring 20." Line 11 and all application text are unchanged, so the specification stays neutral on a direction the disclosure never states.

**Length trims to stay under the limit.** The two additions pushed FIG. 1 to 2847 and FIG. 4 to 2815, so I removed invented rendering constraints rather than required geometry: "of substantial width" from the frame body, "knuckle" from the hinge block, "wholly" from the cutting-line placement, and some redundant phrasing in the latch and carriage sentences. FIG. 1 is now 2799 and FIG. 4 is 2796; FIG. 2, 3, 5 and 6 are untouched at 2757, 2790, 1945 and 2796.

No numeral moved between sheets, no numeral definition changed, and the claims, numeral table, and disclosed embodiments are as they were. The prior-art index remains empty and no search was run, so the Background carries no citations and the art available to this draft may be incomplete.

input.summary: Fixed both reviewer findings. The FIG. 3 section is now indicated conventionally: the FIG. 1 brief gives each end of the cutting-plane line the view-number designation 3, and the Brief Description and detailed description both now read \"taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1\" instead of working around the missing designation. The FIG. 4 brief now carries the direction of wedge advance and the resulting sense of ring movement in its own schematic-depiction list, so a kinematic choice the disclosure is silent on is held as a depiction convention rather than asserted as disclosed structure; line 11 and all application text are unchanged. Both additions pushed their briefs over the 2800-character limit, so I recovered the space by deleting invented rendering constraints rather than required geometry. Claims, numeral table, disclosed embodiments, and the other four briefs are untouched. Prior art note as the brief requires: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and no search was run, so the art available to this draft may be incomplete.
reasoning: The section-designation finding touched three files at once, so I fixed all three rather than only the brief. figures/FIG-1.md now states that each end of the cutting-plane line carries the numeral 3 as the section designation of that view, set just outside the end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3. draft/07-drawings.md and draft/08-detailed-description.md drop the workaround phrase 'taken on the plane indicated by the cutting-plane line and arrows in FIG. 1' for the conventional 'taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1'. The section plane itself was already fully described and consistent between the two sheets, so nothing about the geometry moved.

I added an explicit clause that the 3 is a section designation and not a reference numeral. Without it, a numeral-table check reading the sheet would find a 3 that draft/numerals.md does not define, and the fix for one finding would have manufactured another. The designation is also deliberately kept out of the sheet's numeral list, since that list feeds the deterministic labeller and holds reference numerals only.

The FIG. 4 finding is about where a choice is recorded, not about what is drawn, so I left the geometry alone. The brief still says the wedge's lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and that downward movement drives the band left; what changed is that the schematic list now names 'the direction in which the wedge 52 advances against the ring drive face 36 and the resulting sense of movement of the segmented cam ring 20'. The disclosure says only that the latch drives a wedge against a drive face and rotates the ring through a limited stroke, so the direction is a renderer choice and now reads as one. The application text was already neutral, saying the inclined face converts that advance into circumferential movement, and I did not touch it.

Adding to two briefs that were already near the ceiling took FIG. 1 to 2847 and FIG. 4 to 2815. I recovered the space from invented rendering constraints, which this turn's instructions ask me to remove anyway: 'of substantial width' on the frame body was an invented proportion, 'knuckle' on the hinge block was invented shape detail, 'wholly' on the cutting-line placement was a page-placement constraint, and the latch and carriage sentences carried redundant phrasing. Nothing that identifies a part or states a relationship came out. FIG. 1 is 2799 and FIG. 4 is 2796.

While rewriting the cutting-line sentence I also repaired an ambiguous antecedent: 'a short distance above the outer boundary of that body' followed a sentence whose last-named body was the jaw carriage 30, when the intended reference was the frame body. It now reads 'just outside the outer circle of the frame body', which is the same geometry stated unambiguously.

I made no change to the claims, the numeral table, the disclosed embodiments, or FIG. 2, FIG. 3, FIG. 5 and FIG. 6. The source ledger the reviewer built confirms every limitation and numbered part already traces to the disclosure, so there was nothing to add and any edit there would have been an unnecessary rewrite of settled text.
No numeral changed sheets, so figure-plan coverage stands at eight numerals on FIG. 1 and FIG. 3, seven on FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, four on FIG. 5, and five on FIG. 6, all within the eight-per-sheet limit.

draft/07-drawings.md: FIG. 3 is now 'taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1, which plane contains the radial direction of that jaw carriage and the axis of the frame'.
draft/08-detailed-description.md: the FIG. 3 paragraph now reads 'taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1'.

figures/FIG-4.md: extended the schematic-depiction list to include the direction in which the wedge 52 advances against the ring drive face 36 and the resulting sense of movement of the segmented cam ring 20.

figures/FIG-1.md: removed the invented proportion 'of substantial width' from the annular frame body and 'knuckle' from the hinge block, dropped 'wholly' from the cutting-line placement, and tightened the latch and jaw-carriage sentences, bringing the brief from 2847 to 2799 characters.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there was no document to cite, distinguish, or write around, and I invented none. The Background carries no citations for that reason and the claims rest on the inventor's disclosure alone. The feature carrying claim 1 is the drive element that is divided with the clamp body and recoupled into a single ring by the act of closing the frame halves, through complementary coupling faces at both the hinge end and the latch end, so that one latch input applied at one point on one frame half reaches all three jaw carriages through one kinematic element and the relationship between the carriages is set by ring geometry rather than by how the clamp is operated. The second is the force-limiting spring stack in the drive train between latch handle and wedge, which takes up the handle travel remaining after all three pads land instead of driving one jaw deeper, with the indicator pin reporting the state of that stack and not the diameter of the pipe. Background paragraphs 3, 5 and 7 set out the technical problems both answer, in the invention's own vocabulary rather than that of band clamps or two-bolt saddles, so a later argument has specification support to build on. Nothing this turn narrowed or broadened any claim. Because no search was run, none of this is a statement about what the wider art contains.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending away from it. The latch 16 is in its over-center position, in which the pipe 90 is clamped; the lever attitude is shown schematically.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, each crossing its inner boundary and reaching radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost lies on the first frame half 10 and the other two on the second frame half 12; these positions are shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined to it at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view, on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30. Its outer end lies just outside the outer circle of the frame body and its inner end stops at the concave face of the jaw pad 40 of that carriage, where that face meets the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the left of the view, both to the same side of the line, giving the direction in which the section of FIG. 3 is viewed. Each end also carries the numeral 3 as the section designation of that view, set just outside that end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3; it is not a reference numeral.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer boundary of the frame body at its upper right.

- 90 pipe: target well inside the central circle.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring from the same side as FIG. 1 is viewed, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the even spacing of the three slots and their common tilt, the segment on which the ring drive face 36 lies and its position on the outer boundary, and the length of that face.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20. It is bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the annulus toward the viewer is flat and unbroken except where the three slots described below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus and open at the face toward the viewer, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the width of the annulus and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. The three slots are evenly spaced and identically formed, so that turning the ring a third of a turn carries each slot onto the next and all three tilt the same way about the ring: in each slot the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short flat on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint. There the outer boundary is interrupted by a single straight edge running between two points of that boundary that lie near one another, slanting inward toward that joint and cutting a little material from the segment. Elsewhere the outer boundary of both segments is circular.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary of the annulus in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the straight flat near the right joint.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over that face.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

It is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right, a short arm reaching from that pivot down and left onto the upper end of that stack. The top and right walls stop short of one another, leaving an opening through which the lever runs up and right, leaning past upright, the over-center position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. In this view the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and the radial direction horizontally, radially outward toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and to the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching and the two segment ends are drawn in outline without hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the slight curvature of the upright edges, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the width of the gap.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one filling the lower part, with a narrow horizontal gap between them that runs the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Each of the two bodies is a single body of hatched material, bounded on the left and on the right by upright edges that curve slightly, and ending toward the gap in a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right edge.

A recess is formed in the end face of each body and opens into the gap, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each recess is set back from the left and the right edge of its body, so hatched frame material stands on both sides of it.

An unhatched block sits in each recess and projects from it into the gap. The block held in the upper body and projecting downward is the first cam ring segment 22, and the block held in the lower body and projecting upward is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line with one another.

Midway across the gap the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary horizontal surfaces in contact, so the two blocks read as one upright body interrupted at the joint. Those meeting surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target the hatching of the upper body, left of the recess in it.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatching of the lower body, left of the recess in it.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper unhatched block.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower unhatched block.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces midway across the gap.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts shown in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the attitude of the latch handle 50 in the over-center position, the frame-wall interruption, the length of the ring drive face 36, the width of the gap between the frame bodies, the pivot mounting of the latch handle 50, the opening it passes through, its outline and the short arm by which it acts on the stack, the direction in which the wedge 52 advances against the ring drive face 36 and the resulting sense of movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second holds a like band from the right. A narrow gap separates the bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over that face.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right. The top and right walls stop short of one another, leaving an opening through which the handle runs up and to the right, leaning past upright, the over-center position. From the pivot to its outer end the handle is one straight bar of the same width along its whole length, its two long edges straight and parallel, and its outer end is closed by a short straight edge square across the bar. A separate short arm on the same pivot reaches down and left onto the upper end of that stack.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.

- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts shown in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the attitude of the latch handle 50 in the over-center position, the frame-wall interruption, the length of the ring drive face 36, the width of the gap between the frame bodies, the pivot mounting of the latch handle 50, the opening it passes through, its outline and the short arm by which it acts on the stack, the direction in which the wedge 52 advances against the ring drive face 36 and the resulting sense of movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second holds a like band from the right. A narrow gap separates the bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over that face.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right. The top and right walls stop short of one another, leaving an opening through which the handle runs up and to the right, leaning past upright, the over-center position. From the pivot to its outer end the handle is one straight bar of the same width along its whole length, its two long edges straight and parallel, and its outer end is closed by a short straight edge square across the bar. A separate short arm on the same pivot reaches down and left onto the upper end of that stack.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's left being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as a notch in the segmented cam ring 20 at this plane.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions are shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One short rectangular notch is cut into that block from its left face and stops within it, and apart from that notch the block is solid and hatched throughout. That notch is the oblique slot 34. Hatched material of the block lies above the notch, below it, and right of its closed end. The position of the notch in the block and its depth are shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into the notch in the block, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of that notch, so the only open space left in the notch is the space around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, that is, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 18 annular guide: target the groove wall above the block lying in it.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the block lying in the groove.
- 30 jaw carriage: target the hatching of the block in the channel.
- 32 follower: target well inside the post.
- 34 oblique slot: target the open space of the notch, right of the post.
- 38 radial guide: target the right wall of the channel that receives the jaw carriage 30.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the body hanging below the jaw carriage 30.
- 44 carriage return spring: target the zigzag line.

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's left being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as a notch in the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One short rectangular notch is cut into that block from its left face and stops within it; apart from that notch the block is solid and hatched throughout, with hatched material above the notch, below it and right of its closed end. That notch is the oblique slot 34, its position in the block and its depth shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into that notch, its upper and lower sides facing the notch sides, so the only open space left in the notch is around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 18 annular guide: target the groove wall above the block lying in it.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the block lying in the groove.
- 30 jaw carriage: target the hatching of the block in the channel.
- 32 follower: target well inside the post.
- 34 oblique slot: target the open space of the notch, right of the post.
- 38 radial guide: target the right wall of the channel that receives the jaw carriage 30.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the body hanging below the jaw carriage 30.
- 44 carriage return spring: target the zigzag line.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the even spacing and tilt of the three slots, the segment carrying the ring drive face 36, its position on the outer boundary and its length.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between those two boundaries the face toward the viewer is flat and unbroken except where the three slots below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings open at the face toward the viewer, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. The three are evenly spaced and identically formed, so turning the ring a third of a turn carries each onto the next and all three tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short flat on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint: there a single straight edge runs between two points of that boundary lying near one another, slanting inward toward that joint and cutting a little material from the segment. Elsewhere the outer boundary of both segments is circular.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the straight flat near the right joint.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending away from it. The latch 16 is in its over-center position, the pipe 90 clamped; the lever attitude is shown schematically.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, each crossing its inner boundary and reaching inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost lies on the first frame half 10 and the other two on the second frame half 12; shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view, on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30. Its outer end lies just outside the outer circle of the frame body and its inner end stops where the concave face of the jaw pad 40 of that carriage meets the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the left of the view, both to the same side of the line, giving the direction in which the section of FIG. 3 is viewed. Each end also carries the numeral 3 as the section designation, set just outside that end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3; it is not a reference numeral.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer circle bounding the frame body, at the upper left of the view, away from the pipe 90.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the block of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the topmost carriage inner end.
- 90 pipe: target the interior of the central circle, inside the frame body's inner boundary.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts shown in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the frame-wall interruption, the length of the ring drive face 36, the gap width between the frame bodies, the attitude of the latch handle 50 in the over-center position, its pivot mounting, outline, opening and the short arm by which it acts on the stack, the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the resulting sense of movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second holds a like band from the right. A narrow gap separates the bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over that face.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right and runs up and to the right through an opening left where the top and right walls stop short of one another, leaning past upright, the over-center position. From that pivot to its outer end it is one straight bar of even width, its two long edges straight and parallel, its outer end closed by a straight edge square across the bar. A separate short arm on the same pivot reaches down and left onto the upper end of that stack.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the even spacing and tilt of the three slots, the segment carrying the ring drive face 36, its position on the outer boundary and its length.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between those two boundaries the face toward the viewer is flat and unbroken except where the three slots below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings open at the face toward the viewer, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. The three are evenly spaced and identically formed, so turning the ring a third of a turn carries each onto the next and all three tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short flat on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint: there a single straight edge runs between two points of that boundary lying near one another, slanting inward toward that joint and cutting a little material from the segment. Elsewhere the outer boundary of both segments is circular.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's left being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as a notch in the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One short rectangular notch is cut into that block from its left face and stops within it; apart from that notch the block is solid and hatched throughout, with hatched material above the notch, below it and right of its closed end. That notch is the oblique slot 34, its position in the block and its depth shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into that notch, its upper and lower sides facing the notch sides, so the only open space left in the notch is around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one filling the lower part, with a narrow horizontal gap between them that runs the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Each of the two bodies is a single body of hatched material, bounded on the left and on the right by upright edges that curve slightly, and ending toward the gap in a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right edge.

Midway across the gap the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary horizontal surfaces in contact, so the two blocks read as one upright body interrupted at the joint.
