The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is taken on a plane containing the axis of the frame and corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, the plane of FIG. 5 passing through the mounting boss 70. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing outside the annular guide 18, no part of the mounting boss 70 reaching into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30, so that the frame in the closed condition has the annular guide 18 and three radial guides 38. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the segmented cam ring 20 and to the ring drive face 36.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

# FIG. 5

Enlarged fragmentary sectional view taken on a plane containing the frame axis and corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, passing through the frame at the mounting boss. Radially outward is toward the top of the view, and the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, all of it well inside the drawing area.

A hatched body in section spans the lower part of the view. A groove is formed in it, its proportions and the direction in which it opens shown schematically, bounded by the body on its radially outer side above and its radially inner side below, closed at its right and opening toward the left of the view. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it in the radial direction with a small running clearance at the walls above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20.

A further block projects upward from the upper surface of the body and is joined to the body along its base, standing radially outside the groove so that the radially outer wall of the groove lies between the base of that block and the groove. It is drawn schematically as a plain rectangular block in section, hatched like the body, its placement radially outside the groove likewise shown schematically, and no part of it reaches into the groove. That projecting block is the mounting boss 70.

An upper block rests on the upper end of the mounting boss 70 and is joined to it. It is drawn schematically as a plain rectangle in outline without hatching, and its name is a semantic identifier that does not appear as drawing text. That upper block is the equipment 80.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 18 annular guide: target the wall of the groove above the block that lies in it.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target well inside the hatching of the block lying in the groove.
- 70 mounting boss: target well inside the hatching of the block projecting above the body.
- 80 equipment: target well inside the rectangle resting on the mounting boss 70.

The one finding is fixed in all three loci, and FIG. 1 was left untouched.

FIG. 5 was styled as a sectional view taken on a plane while no cutting plane for it appeared on any other view, unlike FIG. 3, which is anchored by the designated line 3-3 in FIG. 1. The cause is that the mounting boss 70 is optional and deliberately absent from FIG. 1, so there is no view to cut it from. Adding the boss and a section line to FIG. 1 would have required inventing a circumferential location for it, which the disclosure does not supply, so the repair was to the caption rather than to the drawing set.

FIG. 5 is now a fragmentary view with parts shown in section on a plane containing the axis of the frame and corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, worded consistently in the Brief Description of the Drawings, the Detailed Description, and the FIG. 5 brief. That form needs no designated cutting plane. The orientation cross-reference to FIG. 3 is kept, since it is what tells the reader how to read the annular guide 18 and the segmented cam ring 20 in that view, and the plane is still stated to pass through the mounting boss 70 in the description.

FIG. 3 remains the only view designated by a section line, and line 3-3 still agrees across the FIG. 1 brief, the FIG. 3 brief, the Brief Description, and the Detailed Description. Claims, the numeral table, and every other figure brief are unchanged.

input.summary: Fixed the one reported finding by restyling FIG. 5 in all three places it is described. It is now an enlarged fragmentary view with parts shown in section on a plane containing the axis of the frame and corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, rather than a sectional view taken on a plane, so it no longer owes a cutting-plane indication on another view. The wording matches across draft/07-drawings.md, draft/08-detailed-description.md, and figures/FIG-5.md. FIG. 1 was not touched, no cutting-plane line was added, and no circumferential location for the mounting boss was invented. Claims, numeral table, and every other figure brief are unchanged.
reasoning: The defect was a caption-style mismatch between two same-styled views, not a missing drawing. FIG. 3 is anchored by the designated line 3-3 drawn in FIG. 1, while FIG. 5 was captioned the same way with nothing to anchor it. Restyling it as a fragmentary view with parts shown in section removes the obligation, because that form of view is not cut from a designated plane.

I fixed the caption rather than the drawing set because the alternative would have manufactured source. The mounting boss 70 is optional and absent from FIG. 1, so adding it there together with a section line would have required choosing a circumferential position for the boss around the frame. The inventor says only that the frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide, so any such position would be untraced matter added to serve a formality.

I kept the orientation cross-reference to FIG. 3 rather than dropping it with the section styling. It is not a cutting-plane designation; it is what tells the reader that FIG. 5 is read with radially outward toward the top and the axis running left to right, which is how the annular guide 18 and the segmented cam ring 20 in that view are understood. Removing it would have cost the reader the orientation while gaining nothing.

The description keeps the statement that the plane passes through the mounting boss 70. That locates the cut relative to the boss, which is the part FIG. 5 exists to show, without asserting where the boss sits on the frame.

I changed all three loci in one pass. Leaving the Brief Description or the FIG. 5 brief on the old sectional-view wording would have left the drawing description and the figure brief disagreeing about the character of the same view, which is the kind of split the synchronization check reports.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is a fragmentary view with parts shown in section on a plane containing the axis of the frame and corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, that plane passing through the mounting boss 70. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing outside the annular guide 18, no part of the mounting boss 70 reaching into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30, so that the frame in the closed condition has the annular guide 18 and three radial guides 38. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the segmented cam ring 20 and to the ring drive face 36.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

Both findings are fixed, in the FIG. 4 brief and the one description sentence that listed its parts.

**Coupling faces at the latch end.** FIG. 4 shows the clamped, over-center state, and in that state its own drive geometry has opened the latch-end joint: the wedge drives the left band away from the parting line through the whole ring stroke, and abutting complementary faces can push but not pull, so the load path runs around through the hinge-end joint. The brief now has the band ends face one another across the parting line along complementary surfaces, rather than asserting contact there. FIG. 6 is untouched, since it shows the frame halves closed rather than clamped, which is the state in which those faces do meet.

**Numeral 20 on an individual segment.** FIG. 4 draws the two segments as distinct bands at the same joint FIG. 6 shows, so the assembly numeral was landing on a body that FIG. 2 and FIG. 6 number 24. The left band is now the second cam ring segment 24, which is consistent with FIG. 2 placing the ring drive face 36 on segment 24, and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22. The numeral list carries 22 and 24 in place of 20, putting the sheet at eight numerals, and the passing mention of the ring in the schematic list now names it without a numeral so no numeral appears in the brief that the sheet does not label. The Detailed Description's FIG. 4 sentence now names segments 22 and 24, keeping its part list identical to the sheet's.

Numeral 20 stays correct in FIGS. 2, 3, and 5, where the ring is shown whole, and in the description's shape-neutral statements about the coupled ring. Claims, the numeral table, `draft/07-drawings.md`, and the other figure briefs are unchanged.

Also in FIG-4.md the two bands are now numbered as segments rather than as the assembly: the left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22, the numeral list carries 22 and 24 in place of 20, and the schematic list names the segmented cam ring without a numeral. The Detailed Description sentence introducing FIG. 4 now names segments 22 and 24 so its part list still matches the sheet exactly. FIG. 6, the claims, the numeral table, draft/07-drawings.md and the other figure briefs are unchanged.
reasoning: The contact assertion failed against FIG. 4's own kinematics. That sheet fixes the clamped, over-center state, and its wedge drives the left band away from the parting line through the whole ring stroke; abutting complementary faces transmit push and not pull, so in the clamped state the load runs around through the hinge-end joint and the latch-end faces stand apart. Since the stroke has to carry the jaws across a range of pipe diameters and this is an enlarged view, the separation is not a hairline. Saying the ends face one another along complementary surfaces keeps the joint identifiable without instructing the renderer to close a gap the drive has opened.

I did not touch FIG. 6, because the two sheets show different states. FIG. 6 depicts the frame halves closed, which is exactly when closure has brought the faces together and before the latch drives the ring, so contact is correct there. Changing it to match FIG. 4 would have destroyed the one view that shows the coupling the invention turns on.

The description needed no change for that finding. Its statement that the faces are each shaped so one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint is shape-neutral and source-supported, and it does not assert contact in any particular state, so the defect lived entirely in the brief.

On the numeral, FIG. 4 draws the same joint as FIG. 6 with the two segments as separate bands, so an assembly numeral on one band conflicts with the segment numerals the other briefs use for the same bodies. The identification is forced rather than chosen: FIG. 2 puts the ring drive face 36 on segment 24, FIG. 4 puts that face on its left band, so the left band is segment 24 and the right band is segment 22.

Two consequential edits kept the sheet self-consistent. The numeral list now carries 22 and 24 instead of 20, which brings FIG. 4 to eight numerals, at the per-sheet limit but within it; and the schematic list's passing reference to the segmented cam ring 20 dropped its numeral, so the brief no longer names a numeral that the sheet does not label. Numeral 20 remains right in FIGS. 2, 3 and 5, where the ring appears whole and no joint is shown.

I updated the description's FIG. 4 sentence for the same reason the numeral moved: it enumerated the parts that figure shows, and leaving 20 there would have told the reader to look for a callout the sheet no longer carries. draft/07-drawings.md needed nothing, since it names the segmented cam ring in words without a numeral.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the positions and tilt of the three slots, the segment carrying the ring drive face 36, its position on the outer boundary and its length.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between those two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary, the other the outer. The three are alike in form and all tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short flat on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint: there a single straight edge leaves that boundary at a point spaced from the joint and runs toward the joint, slanting steadily inward so that its end nearer the joint lies radially inside the boundary, cutting a little material from the segment, the edge being inclined to the radial direction at that position in the same sense as the face on which the wedge bears in FIG. 4. Elsewhere both outer boundaries are circular.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending away from it, in its over-center position, the pipe 90 clamped; the lever attitude is shown schematically.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. The topmost lies on the first frame half 10, the others on the second frame half 12. At each of the three positions the inner circle of the frame body is interrupted by a radial opening, and the jaw carriage 30 is drawn as a block extending radially inward through that opening from within the body toward the pipe 90, its outer portion within the body and its inner end standing radially inside the inner circle; shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view, on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30. Its outer end lies just outside the outer circle of the frame body and its inner end stops where the concave face of that carriage's jaw pad 40 meets the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the right of the view, both to the same side of the line, giving the direction in which FIG. 3 is viewed. Each end also carries the numeral 3 as the section designation, set just outside that end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3; it is not a reference numeral.

content.text:
Both findings are fixed inside the figure briefs; no application text changed.

**FIG. 2's cross-figure sense clause.** The sentence already fixed the ring drive face 36 completely in FIG. 2's own coordinates: the edge leaves the outer boundary at a point spaced from the joint and slants steadily inward so its end nearer the joint lies radially inside that boundary. The appended reference to "the same sense as the face ... in FIG. 4" pointed at the opposite-hand view, where the same surface reads mirrored on the page, so it instructed the reverse of the incline the sentence had just specified. The clause is deleted and the sentence ends at its own geometry. FIG. 4 still fixes the identical surface independently in its coordinates, and the two now agree.

**FIG. 1's lever attitude.** FIG. 1 gave the renderer no direction for the latch lever while FIG. 4 fixes it precisely, for one part in one state, so FIG. 1 could have been drawn with the lever swung the other way about the latch. It now extends radially outward and inclines toward the first frame half 10, which is what FIG. 4's "up and to the right, leaning past upright" maps to when read from FIG. 1's opposite axial side, and only the lever's form and proportions remain schematic.

I referred to the latch handle by name rather than by numeral 50 in the FIG. 1 brief. FIG. 1 does not label that part and its numeral list is already at eight, so citing the numeral there would have named a callout the sheet does not carry.

The claims, description, Brief Description of the Drawings, numeral table, and the other figure briefs are unchanged.

In figures/FIG-2.md the trailing cross-figure clause tying the ring drive face 36 inclination to the face in FIG. 4 is deleted, so the sentence ends at the geometry it already fixes in FIG. 2's own coordinates; FIG. 4 continues to fix the same surface independently, and the mirrored-view contradiction is gone. In figures/FIG-1.md the latch lever now extends radially outward and inclined toward the first frame half 10, corresponding to the over-center attitude of the latch handle in FIG. 4, with only the lever's form and proportions left schematic. No application text, claim, numeral table entry, or other figure brief changed.
reasoning: The FIG. 2 clause was worse than redundant, it was inverted. FIG. 2 is viewed from FIG. 1's side and FIG. 4 from the opposite side, so one physical surface appears mirrored between them on the page; telling the renderer to match FIG. 4's sense therefore contradicted the incline the same sentence had already specified in FIG. 2's own terms. Deleting the clause was the right cure because each brief already fixes the surface completely and consistently without it, so nothing about the invention is lost.

I deleted rather than rewrote the cross-reference. Restating it correctly, as the opposite sense on the page, would have made the brief depend on a reader tracking two viewing sides to get one edge right, and any later change to either view's handedness would silently break it. Self-contained geometry in each view is what keeps the two sheets independently checkable.

For FIG. 1 the opposite problem applied: an attitude declared schematic with no direction at all is not a depiction convention, it is a licence to draw a conflict, because FIG. 4 pins the same lever in the same over-center state. Mapping FIG. 4's up-and-to-the-right onto FIG. 1's axial side gives radially outward and inclined toward the first frame half 10, so I stated that positively and narrowed the schematic flag to the lever's form and proportions, which genuinely are a drawing choice.

I named the latch handle in words instead of citing numeral 50 in the FIG. 1 brief. FIG. 1 does not label that part, and its numeral list already stands at the eight-per-sheet limit, so a numeral in the prose would have named a callout the sheet cannot carry, which is the same defect the FIG. 4 numeral cleanup removed last turn.

Neither fix touched draft/. The description and claims say nothing about lever attitude or about the drive face's on-page direction, and both findings were conflicts between two briefs, so adding text would have imported drawing conventions into the specification.

1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	Full source ledger traced. Every claim limitation, numbered part, figure-brief structure, relationship, operating condition and variant in the candidate traces to an affirmative passage of the disclosure (which is reproduced verbatim as the single USER turn in input/conversation.md); no untraced technical matter was found, so no critical disclosure_fidelity findings are reported.
4	
5	Ledger highlights (candidate -> source): semicircular halves, hinge end / latch end, three radial jaw carriages in radial guides, pivoting concave jaw pads "without a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter" -> "a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end. Three radial jaw carriages ... Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter." Segmented cam ring 20 / segments 22, 24 / annular guide 18 / coupling faces 26, 28 / follower 32 in oblique slot 34 / wedge 52 on ring drive face 36 / limited stroke / synchronized inward travel / carriage return spring 44 -> the second disclosure paragraph verbatim. Latch first and second over-center positions, force-limiting spring stack 54 between handle 50 and wedge 52, indicator pin 56 moving relative to a fixed edge of latch housing 58 at a predetermined compression range, and "does not measure pipe diameter" (claim 3) -> the third disclosure paragraph. Method claims 13-15 and the Operation section -> the fourth disclosure paragraph, step for step. Mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide, supporting a sensor/tool/conduit, not participating in synchronization, and its optionality ("The frame may carry...") -> the fifth disclosure paragraph; equipment 80 in claim 10 and FIG. 5 traces to "for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit."
6	
7	Depiction conventions were checked against the confinement rule. Generic outlines (hinge as a small circle with blocks, latch as a rectangular block, handle as a straight bar of even width, boss and equipment as plain rectangles, spring stack as one spring symbol, spring 44 as a zigzag, slot positions/tilt, ring-drive-face position and length, form of the meeting surfaces, wedge advance direction, frame-wall interruption) are each expressly listed as "Shown schematically" in the owning figure brief, stay inside the brief, and are not echoed in the claims or description. Neither 07-drawings nor 08-detailed-description contains "by way of example", "any closed outline", or any other statement that broadens an embodiment to justify a renderer's visual choice, so nothing of that kind is reported.
8	
9	Section-line consistency (the named focus) is clean and geometrically correct. The designation "3-3" is used identically in the source-view brief (figures/FIG-1.md: "Each end also carries the numeral 3 as the section designation ... so the line reads as line 3-3; it is not a reference numeral"), the resulting-view brief (figures/FIG-3.md: "taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1"), the Brief Description (draft/07-drawings.md FIG. 3: "taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1"), and the Detailed Description (draft/08 para. beginning "FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view"). The cutting-plane line lies on the radial centre line of the topmost carriage (vertical in FIG. 1) with both arrows perpendicular to it pointing to the page right; that direction of sight yields a resulting view whose right-hand side is the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed, exactly as figures/FIG-3.md states, and whose upward direction is radially outward, also as stated. FIG. 3 is the only view given a section designation; FIG. 4, FIG. 5 and FIG. 6 are fragmentary views with parts in section, and FIG. 5 depicts the optional-boss variant that FIG. 1 does not show, so the absence of further section lines is correct rather than a gap.
10	
11	Cross-figure geometry was verified rather than assumed and is mutually consistent: FIG. 2 (same side as FIG. 1, hinge end left, latch end right, segment 22 upper, segment 24 lower) agrees with FIG. 1's half assignments; FIG. 4, expressly viewed from the opposite side and with radially outward up, correctly places segment 22 (first frame half) on the right and segment 24 on the left; the ring drive face 36 sits on segment 24 adjacent the latch joint in both FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, and its inward slant toward the joint plus the wedge's descending motion drive the ring in the circumferential sense that, given FIG. 2's slot handedness, advances all three followers inward. FIG. 6 (same side as FIG. 1, outward to the right, first frame half above) is a true enlargement of FIG. 1's right-hand joint, and its broken-away near wall is the axially closed wall of the annular guide shown in FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 ("closed at its right and open toward the left"), which is why the cam ring bears no numeral in FIG. 1. Hatching conventions differ between FIG. 4 (bands cut, hatched) and FIG. 6 (segment ends seen behind a break, unhatched) for the correct reason and are stated in each brief.
12

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is a fragmentary view with parts shown in section on a plane containing the axis of the frame and corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, that plane passing through the mounting boss 70. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing outside the annular guide 18, no part of the mounting boss 70 reaching into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30, so that the frame in the closed condition has the annular guide 18 and three radial guides 38. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the first cam ring segment 22, the second cam ring segment 24 and the ring drive face 36.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

Three radial jaw carriages ... Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter." Segmented cam ring 20 / segments 22, 24 / annular guide 18 / coupling faces 26, 28 / follower 32 in oblique slot 34 / wedge 52 on ring drive face 36 / limited stroke / synchronized inward travel / carriage return spring 44 -> the second disclosure paragraph verbatim. Latch first and second over-center positions, force-limiting spring stack 54 between handle 50 and wedge 52, indicator pin 56 moving relative to a fixed edge of latch housing 58 at a predetermined compression range, and "does not measure pipe diameter" (claim 3) -> the third disclosure paragraph. Method claims 13-15 and the Operation section -> the fourth disclosure paragraph, step for step. Mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide, supporting a sensor/tool/conduit, not participating in synchronization, and its optionality ("The frame may carry...") -> the fifth disclosure paragraph; equipment 80 in claim 10 and FIG. 5 traces to "for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit."

- **[minor] Detailed Description makes the wedge 52 part of the latch 16, while the Summary and all claims recite the wedge as a separate element moved by the latch** (draft/08-detailed-description.md, first paragraph under "The latch and the force-limiting drive train"; cf. draft/09-cla) - The description defines the latch 16 as including the wedge 52 among its components. The claims consistently do the opposite: claim 1 recites "a wedge movable by the latch" as an element distinct from the latch, and then recites "the latch comprising a latch handle and a force-limiting spring stack in a drive train between the latch handle and the wedge"; claim 2 adds only "a latch housing and an indicator pin" to the latch; claim 10 repeats the same split. The Summary also keeps the wedge outside the latch ("A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face"). The disclosure likewise treats the wedge as something the latch drives ("Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring"). The result is that the same relationship is expressed two incompatible ways across the specification, and "the latch" would read on different collections of parts in the description and in the claims. The same sentence also uses the definite article for "the drive train" before any drive train has been introduced in the description.
  - Suggested fix: Replace the sentence in draft/08-detailed-description.md with: "The latch 16 comprises a latch housing 58 at the latch end and a latch handle 50, and moves a wedge 52 through a drive train that includes a force-limiting spring stack 54 between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52." No other change is needed; the remainder of that section and the Operation section already describe the wedge 52 only as being advanced and retracted by movement of the latch handle 50.
