1	The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
8	
9	The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is a fragmentary view with parts shown in section on a plane containing the axis of the frame and corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, that plane passing through the mounting boss 70. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing outside the annular guide 18, no part of the mounting boss 70 reaching into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
10	
11	The segmented cam ring
12	
13	FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.
14	
15	The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.
16	
17	Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.
18	
19	The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.
22	
23	The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch 16 acts through a wedge 52 as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge 52 can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which the wedge 52 advances, so that advance of the wedge 52 moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.
24	
25	The jaw carriages
26	
27	FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.
28	
29	The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30, so that the frame in the closed condition has the annular guide 18 and three radial guides 38. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.
30	
31	The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.
32	
33	At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.
34	
35	A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.
36	
37	The latch and the force-limiting drive train
38	
39	The latch 16 comprises a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in a drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52, the wedge 52 being movable by the latch 16. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.
40	
41	FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the first cam ring segment 22, the second cam ring segment 24 and the ring drive face 36.
42	
43	The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.
44	
45	The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.
46	
47	The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.
48	
49	Operation
50	
51	To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.
52	
53	The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.
54	
55	To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
56	
57	Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch 16 acts through a wedge 52 as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge 52 can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which the wedge 52 advances, so that advance of the wedge 52 moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.

Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

The latch 16 comprises a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in a drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52, the wedge 52 being movable by the latch 16. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. # FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are seen. In this view the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and the radial direction horizontally, radially outward toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching, and each of the two segment ends carries section hatching of its own at a different slant from the frame hatching, so that each segment end reads as a solid body distinct from the frame holding it. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the curvature of the upright edges, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the frame material shown radially outside each channel, the fragment being broken away radially outward short of the frame wall interrupted in FIG. 4.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one filling the lower part, and a single horizontal parting line runs the full width of the view between them. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Each of the two bodies is bounded on the left by an upright edge that curves slightly, on the right by an irregular break line short of the radially outer wall of the frame, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body and from the break line at its right, so hatched frame material stands on both sides of it.

A solid hatched block fills each channel and reaches along it to the end face of the body, ending flush with that end face. The block held in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block held in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand one directly above the other.

The two blocks touch at the parting line: the lower end of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end of the second cam ring segment 24 lie on that one horizontal line, meeting face to face along it with no open space between them, so the two blocks read as one upright body interrupted only at the joint. Those meeting surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target the hatching of the upper body in the material lying to the left of its channel.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatching of the lower body in the material lying to the right of its channel, between that channel and the break line.
- 18 annular guide: target the right-hand wall of the channel in the upper body, where the hatched material of that body meets the right-hand side of the block held in it.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching of the upper block, well away from the parting line.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching of the lower block, well away from the parting line.

content.content: Contains simple_expansion

1	Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.
2	
3	A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.
4	
5	Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.
6	
7	What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
8

1	A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.
2	
3	In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring, so that movement of the latch rotates the coupled ring through the stroke, and a carriage return spring biases each jaw carriage outwardly so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws.
4	
5	Because the coupled ring is a single kinematic element spanning both frame halves, the three jaw carriages are not driven independently. One latch motion, applied at one point on one frame half, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the jaw pads close on the pipe together. The pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter.
6	
7	In a further aspect, the latch has a first position in which the frame halves are held around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which the wedge drives the cam ring and the pipe is clamped, and a force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive train between a latch handle and the wedge. Travel of the handle that remains after all three jaw pads have contacted the pipe compresses the force-limiting spring stack instead of advancing one jaw carriage farther than the others. An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report of clamp loading that is produced by the state of the spring stack and not by the diameter of the pipe.
8	
9	In a further aspect, the frame carries a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool, or a conduit, the mounting boss not participating in the advance of the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism, so that equipment carried on the frame is outside the path by which the jaws are synchronized.
10	
11	In a further aspect, a method of clamping a pipe comprises opening the latch, swinging the frame halves apart about the hinge, placing the frame halves around a pipe, closing the frame halves so that the complementary coupling faces engage and couple the cam ring segments, moving the latch to the first position, and moving the latch to the second, over-center position so that the wedge rotates the coupled ring and the followers advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism until the jaw pads seat on the pipe. Releasing the latch unloads the force-limiting spring stack and the carriage return springs retract the jaw carriages before the frame halves are opened.
12

content.text:
All four flagged sheets are now consistent. Here's what I found and did.

**FIG. 6 (rewritten by me).** Three defects fixed:
- The two segment ends were specified as *unhatched* blocks lying in the guide channels, which the renderer read as void, so they came out as empty white space. They now carry their own section hatching at a slant different from the frame hatching, matching how the cam ring is already drawn in FIG. 3 and FIG. 4, and each block is bounded by its own outline.
- The coupling faces are stated as being in contact across the full width of the blocks at a single parting line.
- The leader anchors for `18` and `22` no longer collide: `18` now targets the hatched band on the radially outer side of the upper channel, `22` the hatching well inside the upper block away from the parting line. `28` has an explicit anchor on the horizontal contact between the two end faces.

**FIG. 1, 2 and 4.** When I went to apply edits, these files already contained wording that resolves the reviewer's findings (pipe drawn as one circle with a broad open band out to the frame's inner circle; hinge confined within the radial width of the frame body; the ring drive face defined by its two endpoints rather than by a slant word). I checked them against the findings and against each other rather than rewriting them: FIG. 2 puts the deep end of the flat at the end nearer the latch joint and runs it out to the outer boundary away from the joint, and FIG. 4, which is the mirrored view, puts the low end of the same face toward the parting line and the high end to the left, with the wedge underside on the same slant so downward wedge travel drives the band circumferentially. Those two descriptions agree, so I left them alone.

No specification text needed changing: the slant directions the reviewer quoted live only in the figure briefs, not in the detailed description, and the description states the drive relationship functionally ("at an inclination to the direction in which the wedge 52 advances"). Numerals, figure lists, citations (the index lists no references) and marker checks are clean.

input.summary: Corrective QA pass on the drawing specifications only. FIG. 6 was rewritten to fix all three reviewer findings: the cam ring segment ends now carry their own section hatching at a slant different from the frame hatching so they read as solid bodies rather than as voids in the guide channels; the two coupling faces are stated as being in contact across the full width of the blocks at one parting line; and the leader anchors were separated so that 18 (outer band of the upper channel wall) and 22 (hatching well inside the upper block) no longer share coordinates, with 28 given an explicit anchor on the horizontal contact between the two end faces. FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 already carried wording that resolves their findings when I opened them to edit (pipe as a single circle with a broad open band out to the frame inner circle, hinge confined within the radial width of the frame body, ring drive face defined by the height of its two ends instead of a slant word). I verified those three against the findings and against one another instead of rewriting them, and left them untouched. No specification text was changed: the slant statements the reviewer attributed to the specification appear only in the figure briefs, and the detailed description states the wedge and drive face relationship functionally. Numerals table, per sheet numeral lists, marker and em dash checks are clean; the prior art index lists no references, so no citation work applied.
reasoning: The reviewer's FIG. 6 complaint about 'empty white space' came from specifying the segment ends as unhatched blocks filling a hatched channel: an unhatched region enclosed by hatched material reads as a hole. Hatching them at a different slant is standard practice for a separate part, is consistent with FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 where the segmented cam ring is already hatched, and does not add any structure to the invention.

The gap the renderer left at the latch-end joint defeats the point of the sheet, which exists to show that closing the frame halves brings the coupling faces together. I stated the contact positively (faces lying against one another across the full width of the blocks at one parting line) rather than banning a gap, because a positive geometric statement is what the geometry pass acts on.

Leader collision between 18 and 22 was structural: both anchors pointed into the same channel region of the upper body. Moving 18 to the band of frame material on the radially outer side of the channel keeps it on the annular guide wall, which is genuinely the guide, while freeing the block interior for 22. The 22 and 24 anchors are held away from the parting line so 28 has clear room, which is why 28 previously failed to place.

FIG. 1, 2 and 4 already contained the corrected wording when I went to edit them. I checked the corrected FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 against each other rather than assuming: FIG. 2 puts the deep end of the flat at the end nearer the latch joint and runs it out to the outer boundary away from the joint; FIG. 4 is the mirrored view and puts the low end of the same face toward the parting line, with the wedge underside on the same slant, so downward wedge travel pushes the band circumferentially. Those agree, so rewriting them would have risked reintroducing the ambiguity.

I did not touch the detailed description. The slant directions the reviewer quoted as coming from the specification are only in the figure briefs; the description says the ring drive face lies at an inclination to the direction in which the wedge advances, which is source faithful and view independent. Changing good text to match a renderer error would be the wrong repair, since the rule is that the text governs the figure and not the reverse.

Nothing in the claims, summary, background or abstract was reopened. The request is corrective QA on the saved candidate, and the review raised no text defect, so the source approved wording stands as filed.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the latch housing and its cavity, the interruption in the frame wall, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude and mounting of the latch handle 50 and the manner in which it acts on the force-limiting spring stack 54, the spring stack drawn as one spring symbol, and the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the resulting movement of the bands.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second hatched body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing the upper side of that band. Near the right end of that exposed side the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface: its left end is the higher, at the level of the exposed upper side, and its right end is the lower, down within the band, so the face descends steadily from left to right, toward the parting line. Its right end stops short of that line, a short piece of the exposed upper side running on from it to the line.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward over the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity above the ring drive face 36; its lower face descends from left to right at the same slant and rests on the ring drive face 36 along its length, so downward movement of the wedge 52 presses the left band toward the left.

Above the wedge 52 the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot, so the stack lies between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening where the top and right walls stop short of one another, leaning past upright, the over-center position; from the pivot to its outer end it is a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, which surface is the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which the position of the indicator pin 56 is read.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching of the right band.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching, and each segment end carries section hatching of its own at a slant different from that of the frame hatching, so that each segment end reads as a solid body distinct from the frame material holding it. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the break running radially outward short of the frame wall interrupted in FIG. 4.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one the lower part, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body and from the break line at its right, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the left edge and a further band stands between the channel and the break line.

A solid block lies in each channel, filled with its own hatching. Each block is bounded by its own outline, has one long edge facing the left wall of its channel and one long edge facing the right wall, and reaches along its channel to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another, in contact across the full width of the blocks, so the two blocks together fill the parting line where they meet and read as one upright body interrupted at the joint. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and its left edge.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the lower body and its left edge.
- 18 annular guide: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and the break line at its right, that band being the wall on the radially outer side of the channel.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the upper body, away from the parting line.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the lower body, away from the parting line.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the horizontal contact between the end faces of the two blocks at the parting line.

content.text:
The gate's single finding was FIG. 4's brief at 2868 characters against a 2800 limit. Fixed.

**FIG. 4** now measures about 2698 characters of brief text. I cut only redundancy, not geometry: the "shown schematically" list was condensed, the ring drive face sentence tightened while keeping both endpoint heights and the descent toward the parting line, and a duplicated "above the ring drive face 36" removed from the wedge sentence. The wedge underside slant, its contact along the ring drive face, and the resulting leftward push on the band are all still stated.

**FIG. 6** got a small cleanup in the same pass: "Each block is bounded by its own outline" was a generic face-linework control, so it is gone, and the coupling sentence now stops at the physical fact (the two end faces in contact across the full width of the blocks, filling the parting line where they meet) instead of narrating how it should read. The different-slant hatching that makes each segment end a solid body stays in the view statement, and the numeral anchors match it.

All six briefs are now within the limit (2363, 2313, 2183, 2698, 1674, 2653 characters), no sheet lists more than eight numerals, every listed numeral is in the table, and the claims, description, drawing descriptions and numeral table are untouched and in step.

input.summary: Fixed the one mechanical failure, the FIG. 4 brief exceeding the 2800 character limit at 2868. FIG. 4 is now about 2698 characters: the shown schematically list was condensed, the ring drive face sentence tightened while keeping both endpoint heights and its descent toward the parting line, and a duplicated statement of the wedge sitting above the ring drive face removed. No geometry, contact, opening or relationship was dropped. In the same pass FIG. 6 lost a generic face linework control (each block bounded by its own outline) and the narration at the end of the coupling sentence, leaving the positive physical statement that the two end faces are in contact across the full width of the blocks and fill the parting line where they meet; its different slant hatching statement and its separated numeral anchors are unchanged. All six briefs now measure 2363, 2313, 2183, 2698, 1674 and 2653 characters of brief text, every sheet lists eight numerals or fewer, every listed numeral is defined once in the table, and the claims, detailed description, drawing descriptions and numeral table were not touched.
reasoning: The length overrun had to be paid for out of wording that carries no geometry, so I took it from the shown schematically disclaimer list and from two duplicated phrases. The physical content the renderer acts on is unchanged: the ring drive face still has a high left end at the level of the exposed upper side and a low right end within the band, still descends toward the parting line, still stops short of that line, and the wedge underside still lies on it at the same slant so that downward wedge travel pushes the band circumferentially.

I did not touch the latch handle or indicator pin sentences, which had already been shortened on disk, and I left the wedge advance clause that had been re-added to the schematic list, taking the on disk state as current rather than reverting it. Trimming elsewhere gave enough margin without undoing another edit.

In FIG. 6 the phrase requiring each block to be bounded by its own outline is exactly the kind of generic face linework control that should not be in a brief; the blocks are already distinguished by their own hatching at a slant different from the frame hatching, which is a positive physical depiction statement, so removing the outline instruction loses nothing and removes an invented rendering constraint.

The tail of the FIG. 6 coupling sentence told the renderer how the drawing should read rather than what is there. The invention fact is contact between the two end faces at the latch end, so the sentence now ends on that contact and on the identification of those surfaces as the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Nothing in the patent text was altered. The finding was a brief length limit, not a defect in the invention as described, so the claims, numeral table, drawing descriptions and detailed description stay exactly as filed and remain in step with the six briefs.

figures/FIG-6.md: removed the generic instruction that each block be bounded by its own outline, the blocks remaining distinguished by their own hatching at a slant different from the frame hatching

figures/FIG-6.md: the latch end coupling sentence now ends on the physical contact of the two end faces across the full width of the blocks, without the trailing description of how the pair should read
input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite or distinguish and the Background carries no citations. The claims are unchanged and continue to rest on the disclosed combination the inventor calls essential: a cam ring split with the frame and recoupled by the act of closing it so one latch input reaches all three carriages through a single coupled ring, oblique slot and follower pairs that turn that one rotation into synchronized radial travel, and a force limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge that absorbs the operator's remaining handle travel instead of driving one jaw harder than the others. The Background states the technical problem each of those solves.

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching, and each segment end carries section hatching of its own at a slant different from that of the frame hatching, so that each segment end reads as a solid body distinct from the frame material holding it. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the break running radially outward short of the frame wall interrupted in FIG. 4.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one the lower part, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body and from the break line at its right, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the left edge and a further band stands between the channel and the break line.

A solid block filled with its own hatching lies in each channel, one long edge facing the left wall of its channel and one long edge facing the right wall, and reaches along its channel to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another, in contact across the full width of the blocks, so the two blocks together fill the parting line where they meet. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and its left edge.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the lower body and its left edge.
- 18 annular guide: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and the break line at its right, that band being the wall on the radially outer side of the channel.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the upper body, away from the parting line.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the lower body, away from the parting line.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the horizontal contact between the end faces of the two blocks at the parting line.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching, and each segment end carries section hatching of its own at a slant different from that of the frame hatching. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the extent of the break at the radially outer side of each body.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one the lower part, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and that edge. In the upper body a further band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the break line at its right. In the lower body the frame wall radially outside the channel is interrupted, as in FIG. 4, so the radially outer side of the block in that channel is exposed, the break line at the right of that body lying beyond that exposed side.

A solid block filled with its own hatching lies in each channel and reaches along it to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another in contact across the full width of the blocks, filling the parting line where they meet. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and its left edge.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the lower body and its left edge.
- 18 annular guide: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and the break line at its right, that band being the wall on the radially outer side of the channel.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the upper body, away from the parting line.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the lower body, away from the parting line.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the horizontal contact between the end faces of the two blocks at the parting line.

**What changed in `figures/FIG-6.md`:**
- The schematic list no longer asserts that the break stops short of the wall FIG. 4 shows interrupted; it now covers the extent of the break at the radially outer side of each body.

That matches FIG. 4, where the wedge reaches the ring drive face through exactly that interruption.
- The block sentence no longer claims a right-hand channel wall facing each block, which would have contradicted the interruption in the lower body. The blocks are still solid and hatched, still reach to the end face of their body, and still meet in contact across their full width at the parting line.

The numeral notes are unchanged, as the reviewer indicated: 18 targets the upper body's outer band, which is still present, and 10 and 12 target the inner bands, present in both bodies. No change was needed to the claims, detailed description, drawing descriptions, numeral table, or FIG. 4.

Added text was paid for by removing duplication, so all six briefs stay under the length limit at 2363, 2313, 2183, 2698, 1674 and 2664 characters.
reasoning: The conflict was real and one sided: FIG. 4 needs the frame wall radially outside the second cam ring segment 24 interrupted, because that interruption is how the wedge in the latch housing reaches the ring drive face at all. FIG. 6 depicts the same joint, so FIG. 6 is the sheet that had to yield, and the interruption is now stated there for the lower body only, which is the frame half that carries that segment.

The upper body keeps its outer band of frame material. Nothing in the disclosure or the description says the guide wall is interrupted anywhere but where the wedge acts, so extending the interruption to both bodies would have invented structure, and removing the band entirely would have orphaned the anchor for the annular guide 18.

I dropped the clause giving each block a right-hand channel wall to face. SOURCE LEDGER - traced every claim limitation, every numeral, and every specific structure, relationship, result, position, connection, operating condition, and variant in draft/04 through draft/10, numerals.md, and figures/FIG-1..6.md to the inventor text. The disclosure and the single USER passage in conversation.md are identical in substance, so both were used as the authority.

Supported and traced (representative mapping): reusable split pipe clamp 100 / "A reusable split pipe clamp"; semicircular halves 10, 12 / "a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half"; hinge 14 and releasable latch 16 at opposite ends / "joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end"; three jaw carriages 30 in three radial guides 38 / "Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame. Each carriage slides in a radial guide"; pivoting concave jaw pad 40 and diameter-independence / "carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter"; segmented cam ring 20 in annular guide 18 / "A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame"; segments 22, 24 one per half / "One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half"; complementary coupling faces 26, 28 at hinge and latch ends and their engagement on closing and separation on opening (claims 1, 7, 10, 13) / "When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring"; follower 32 in oblique slot 34 and synchronized inward travel / "Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages"; wedge 52 on ring drive face 36 and limited stroke / "Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke"; carriage return springs 44 (claims 1, 10, 15) / "A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released"; first/over-center latch positions (claims 4, 12, 13) / "The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe"; force-limiting spring stack 54 between handle 50 and wedge 52 (claims 1, 10, 13) / "A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others"; indicator pin 56, latch housing 58, fixed edge, predetermined compression range, diameter-independence (claims 2, 3, 11, 14) / "A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range... does not measure pipe diameter"; method claims 13-15 / the install-and-remove paragraph; mounting boss 70 and equipment 80 as sensor, tool or conduit, outside the annular guide, not participating in synchronization (claims 8, 10) / "The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization." Title, applicant/inventor, "Not applicable" cross-reference and government-support statements match input/brief.md. Background prior-art characterizations were not traced, per scope.

Depiction conventions checked and accepted as confined to the figure briefs, each flagged "shown schematically" in its brief, with the application text and claims left shape-neutral: hinge 14 as a small circle with short blocks; latch 16 as a rectangular block with a lever; latch housing 58 and its cavity; latch handle 50 as a straight bar; the frame-wall interruption over segment 24; the direction in which annular guide 18 opens; spring 44 as a zigzag; mounting boss 70 as a plain rectangular block; equipment 80 as an unhatched rectangle; carriage positions at top, lower left, lower right. No "by way of example", "any closed outline", or similar embodiment-broadening sentence appears anywhere in draft/, and no drafting note, placeholder, open question, instruction, or unresolved alternative remains.

Cross-document consistency verified: all 26 numerals in numerals.md are used in draft/08 and appear in at least one figure brief; each numeral carries exactly one meaning everywhere; the figure-by-figure numeral sets in draft/08 match the "Numerals shown on this figure" lists exactly; claims and description use identical relationship language.

SECTION-LINE CHECK (the named focus): the only designated section line is 3-3. It carries the same designation in the source view (figures/FIG-1.md: "Each end carries the numeral 3 as the section designation... so the line reads as line 3-3"), in the resulting view (figures/FIG-3.md: "taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1"), in the Brief Description (draft/07-drawings.md line 5), and in the detailed description (draft/08 line 27). The arrow sense is also geometrically consistent: FIG. 1's arrows point to the right of a vertical radial line, which for a view with radially outward up places the FIG.-1 viewing side at the right of FIG. 3, exactly as figures/FIG-3.md states. The kinematics agree across figures as well: the wedge in FIG. 4 drives segment 24 away from the latch joint, which is clockwise as seen in FIGS. 1 and 2, and the FIG. 2 slot tilt ("the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary") converts that clockwise rotation into inward carriage travel. FIGS. 4 and 6 place the frame-wall interruption on the same frame half, and the left/right and up/down assignments of segments 22 and 24 in FIGS. 2, 4 and 6 are mutually consistent with their stated viewing sides. FIGS. 4, 5 and 6 are fragmentary/broken-out views rather than sections taken on a line of another figure, so no further section-line designation is required.

One inconsistency found: the Brief Description of FIG. 6 limits the sectioning at the break to the frame, while the FIG. 6 brief also hatches the two cam ring segments. Reported below as minor. No unsupported disclosure matter was found.

## Reviewer findings

- **[minor] Brief Description of FIG. 6 sections only the frame, but the FIG. 6 brief also hatches the two cam ring segments** (draft/07-drawings.md line 11 vs. figures/FIG-6.md lines 3 and 9 (and the numeral targets at lines 18-19)) - The Brief Description states that at the break only the frame is shown in section, and that the break makes the segment ends merely visible. The figure brief, however, applies section hatching to the cam ring segments as well and directs the lead lines for 22 and 24 at that hatching. As written, the two documents disagree about which parts are cut at the break: a part exposed by a break rather than cut by it is drawn in outline, so a reader comparing the Brief Description with the figure cannot tell whether the segment ends are cut surfaces or exposed faces. This is a text-versus-figure-brief mismatch only; the underlying structure (segment ends meeting at the coupling faces 28 with the near frame wall removed) is fully supported by the disclosure and is described consistently in draft/08 line 15.
  - Suggested fix: In draft/07-drawings.md, replace "and the frame shown in section at the break" with "and the frame and the cam ring segments shown in section at the break", so the Brief Description matches the two-slant hatching already specified in figures/FIG-6.md. (Equivalently, if the segments are intended to be exposed rather than cut, amend figures/FIG-6.md instead: change "and each segment end carries section hatching of its own at a slant different from that of the frame hatching" to "and the exposed segment ends are drawn in outline without hatching", change "A solid block filled with its own hatching" to "A solid block drawn in outline", and change the 22 and 24 targets to "target well inside the block ... away from the parting line". Adopt one of the two, not both.)

Fix every listed item before returning. If an advisory is a false positive, make
the wording or figure specification unambiguous enough that the check passes.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching, and each segment end carries section hatching of its own at a slant different from that of the frame hatching. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the extent of the break at the radially outer side of each body.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one the lower part, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and that edge. In the upper body a further band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the break line at its right. In the lower body the frame wall radially outside the channel is interrupted, as in FIG. 4, so the radially outer side of the block in that channel is exposed, the break line at the right of that body lying beyond that exposed side.

A solid block filled with its own hatching lies in each channel and reaches along it to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another in contact across the full width of the blocks, filling the parting line where they meet. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and its left edge.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the lower body and its left edge.
- 18 annular guide: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and the break line at its right, that band being the wall on the radially outer side of the channel.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the upper body, away from the parting line.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the lower body, away from the parting line.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the horizontal contact between the end faces of the two blocks at the parting line.

content.text:
The one finding was the mismatch between the Brief Description of FIG. 6 and the FIG. 6 brief over what is cut at the break. Fixed by adopting the first of the two alternatives, which keeps the hatching that makes the segment ends read as solid bodies.

**`draft/07-drawings.md`** now reads that FIG. 6 is viewed with the near frame wall broken away "and the frame and the cam ring segments shown in section at the break," matching the two-slant hatching in the brief.

**`figures/FIG-6.md`** opening sentence was aligned to the same statement: the frame and the two cam ring segments are shown in section at the break so that the segment ends are seen. The rest of the brief is unchanged, so the segment ends still carry hatching at a slant different from the frame hatching, and the leaders for 22 and 24 still land on that hatching.

Nothing else moved: the detailed description's account of FIG. 6 makes no statement about what is cut, and the claims, numeral table and FIG. 4 were untouched. FIG. 6's brief is 2717 characters and FIG. 4's is 2698, both inside the limit, with the other four at 2363, 2313, 2183 and 1674.

input.summary: Fixed the single reported inconsistency, the disagreement between the Brief Description of FIG. 6 and the FIG. 6 brief about which parts are cut at the break. draft/07-drawings.md now states that the frame and the cam ring segments are shown in section at the break, matching the two slant hatching already specified in figures/FIG-6.md, and the opening sentence of figures/FIG-6.md was aligned to the same statement so that both documents say the frame and the two cam ring segments are shown in section at the break and the segment ends are seen. The rest of the FIG. 6 brief is unchanged: the segment ends keep section hatching at a slant different from the frame hatching, which is what makes them read as solid bodies rather than as voids in the guide channels, and the leaders for 22 and 24 still land on that hatching. The detailed description says nothing about what is cut at the break, so no change was needed there, and the claims, numeral table and FIG. 4 were untouched. FIG. 6's brief measures 2717 characters and FIG. 4's 2698, with the remaining four at 2363, 2313, 2183 and 1674, all inside the limit.
reasoning: The finding offered two mutually exclusive cures, and I took the one that keeps the hatching. Returning the segment ends to plain outline would undo the fix that stopped them rendering as empty space inside the hatched channels, so the cheaper correction was to bring the Brief Description into line with the brief rather than the other way round.

I changed the brief's own first sentence as well, because it still said the break made the segment ends visible while a later sentence hatched them. 1	Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.
2	
3	A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.
4	
5	Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.
6	
7	What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
8

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown, the frame and the two cam ring segments being shown in section at the break so that the segment ends are seen. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching, and each segment end carries section hatching of its own at a slant different from that of the frame hatching. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the extent of the break at the radially outer side of each body.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one the lower part, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and that edge. In the upper body a further band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the break line at its right. In the lower body the frame wall radially outside the channel is interrupted, as in FIG. 4, so the radially outer side of the block in that channel is exposed, the break line at the right of that body lying beyond that exposed side.

A solid block filled with its own hatching lies in each channel and reaches along it to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another in contact across the full width of the blocks, filling the parting line where they meet. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

- 10 first frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and its left edge.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the lower body and its left edge.
- 18 annular guide: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and the break line at its right, that band being the wall on the radially outer side of the channel.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the upper body, away from the parting line.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the lower body, away from the parting line.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the horizontal contact between the end faces of the two blocks at the parting line.
