Two of the three findings were file-level and are fixed; the third is a rendering gap.

**Background (`draft/05-background.md`).** The unsourced prior-art specifics are gone. The pull-closed sentence no longer names particular constructions and now ends with the supported point: an arrangement of that kind depends on a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, so a different pipe size calls for a different part. The damage sentence and the named instruments are replaced by what the disclosure supports: concentrated loading of a single gripping surface is undesirable and the operator has no indication that it has occurred, and an added instrument that responds to the position of the gripping elements reports the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip. input.old_string: Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. An arrangement of that kind depends on a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, so that a different pipe size calls for a different part.

tool_use_result.originalFile:
Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.

A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. An arrangement of that kind depends on a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, so that a different pipe size calls for a different part.

Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Concentrated loading of a single gripping surface is undesirable, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. An added instrument that responds to the position of the gripping elements reports the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.

What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching, the wedge 52, the latch housing 58 and each cam ring segment each at a slant different from that of the frame bodies that hold them; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity, the interruption in the frame wall, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude and mounting of the latch handle 50, its action on the force-limiting spring stack 54, that stack drawn as one spring symbol, and the direction in which the wedge 52 advances with the resulting movement of the bands.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second hatched body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing the upper side of that band. Near the right end of that exposed side the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface, its left end high at the level of the exposed upper side and its right end low within the band, so the face descends from left to right, toward the parting line. Its right end stops short of that line, a short piece of the exposed upper side running on from it to the line.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward over the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity; its lower face descends from left to right at the same slant and rests on the ring drive face 36 along its length, so downward movement of the wedge 52 presses the left band toward the left.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot, so the stack lies between them.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening where the top and right walls stop short of one another, leaning past upright, the over-center position; it is a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which its position is read.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching of the right band.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

Both file-level findings are fixed; the third is the empty drawing set.

**Hatching slants (`figures/FIG-3.md`, `figures/FIG-4.md`).** Each now states the distinction FIG. 6 already carried. FIG. 3: cut material carries hatching, with the segmented cam ring 20 and the jaw carriage 30 each at a slant different from the frame body that holds them, so the ring reads as free to move circumferentially in the annular guide 18 and the carriage as free to slide in the radial guide 38. FIG. 4: the wedge 52, the latch housing 58 and each cam ring segment each at a slant different from the frame bodies that hold them. To keep FIG. 4 inside the length limit I removed only redundancy: a repeated naming of the handle and wedge around the spring stack, a schematic clause duplicating the wedge direction that the body already states positively, and a wordy description of the housing opening.

**Background (`draft/05-background.md`).** The two sentences are now conditional statements of the engineering problem rather than assertions about existing arrangements: if the gripping surfaces of each part are driven separately, the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive is given up, with the consequences that follow; if the split body is instead pulled closed on the pipe, the closing force passes through the joint at the split and the pipe reacts the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore matches the pipe and a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is needed. Nothing the disclosure supports was lost, and the closing paragraph still frames what the coupled ring and the spring stack solve.

**Rendered sheets.** `figures/` still holds only the six Markdown briefs. Figure files are specifications and the sheets are produced by the image pipeline, so I created no image files and removed no "shown in FIG. N" passage or numeral definition. The briefs cover every reported numeral: 100, 10, 12, 14, 16, 30, 40, 90 on FIG. 1; 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 34, 36 on FIG. 2; 18, 20, 30, 32, 34, 38, 40, 44 on FIG. 3; 22, 24, 36, 50, 52, 54, 56, 58 on FIG. 4; 18, 20, 70, 80 on FIG. 5; 10, 12, 18, 22, 24, 28 on FIG. 6.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is a fragmentary view with parts shown in section on a plane containing the axis of the frame and corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, that plane passing through the mounting boss 70. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing outside the annular guide 18, no part of the mounting boss 70 reaching into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch 16 acts through a wedge 52 as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge 52 can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which the wedge 52 advances, so that advance of the wedge 52 moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30, so that the frame in the closed condition has the annular guide 18 and three radial guides 38. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

The latch 16 comprises a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in a drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52, the wedge 52 being movable by the latch 16. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the first cam ring segment 22, the second cam ring segment 24 and the ring drive face 36.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body carry hatching at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches or lies beside in the view; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity, the interruption in the frame wall, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude and mounting of the latch handle 50, its action on the force-limiting spring stack 54, that stack drawn as one spring symbol, and the direction in which the wedge 52 advances.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second hatched body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing the upper side of that band. Near the right end of that exposed side the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface, its left end high at the level of the exposed upper side and its right end low within the band, so the face descends from left to right, toward the parting line. Its right end stops short of that line, a short piece of the exposed upper side running on from it to the line.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward over the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity; its lower face descends from left to right at the same slant and rests on the ring drive face 36 along its length, so downward movement of the wedge 52 presses the left band toward the left.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot, so the stack lies between them.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening between the top and right walls, leaning past upright, the over-center position; it is a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which its position is read.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching of the right band.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown, the frame and the two cam ring segments being shown in section at the break so that the segment ends are seen. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut material carries section hatching; the upper frame body, the lower frame body and each of the two cam ring segments carry hatching at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches, so the parting line and the contact between the segment end faces stay distinct. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the extent of the break at the radially outer side of each body.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, filling the upper and lower parts of the view, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and that edge. In the upper body a further band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the break line at its right. In the lower body the frame wall radially outside the channel is interrupted, as in FIG. 4, so the radially outer side of the block in that channel is exposed, the break line at the right of that body lying beyond that exposed side.

A solid block lies in each channel and reaches along it to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another in contact across the full width of the blocks, filling the parting line where they meet. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and its left edge.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the lower body and its left edge.
- 18 annular guide: target the surface of the channel wall in the upper body on the radially outer side of the block that lies in the channel.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the upper body, away from the parting line.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the lower body, away from the parting line.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the horizontal contact between the end faces of the two blocks at the parting line.

reasoning: The hatching rule was stated only against the frame, which left the pairs that matter unprotected: the wedge sits inside and bears on the latch housing, the two frame bodies meet at the parting line, and in FIG. 6 the two segment ends touch at the very interface the sheet exists to show. Stating the requirement pairwise, against every cut element a body touches or lies beside, covers those pairs without naming a slant for any of them, which keeps the brief free of invented rendering values.

In FIG. 6 I kept the reason in the sentence, that the parting line and the segment contact stay distinct, because the requirement and its purpose travel together: a renderer that knows why the slants must differ is less likely to merge the two blocks into one body, which was the earlier failure mode on that sheet.

The FIG. 2 wording was a genuine internal contradiction rather than a drawing artifact. The description defines the coupled condition as made by closing the frame halves and broken by opening them, so a ring drawn outside the frame cannot be in it. The isolated-subassembly phrasing keeps the figure showing exactly the same geometry, the segment ends meeting at the coupling faces, without asserting a state the specification says cannot exist there.

Both edits added characters to briefs that had little headroom, so I paid for them out of duplication rather than geometry. The wedge direction clause in the FIG. 4 schematic list was worse than redundant, since the downward advance and the resulting leftward push are required relationships stated positively in the body, and flagging that direction as schematic worked against the text.

Nothing in the claims or the numeral table moved, and the only description change is the FIG. 2 sentence, which the finding identified. The one file-level finding is fixed, and the drawing set is now consistent on hatching across every sectioned sheet.

**`figures/FIG-3.md`.** The hatching rule now reads that the frame body, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriage 30 with its follower 32, and the jaw pad 40 each carry hatching at a slant different from every other cut element it touches or lies beside in the view. That covers the two contacts the brief creates in the cutting plane: the follower sitting inside the oblique slot 34 with their surfaces facing, and the jaw pad hanging on the lower end of the carriage.

**`figures/FIG-5.md`.** I applied the same rule there, since that sheet also shows cut parts in contact: the segmented cam ring 20 lies in the groove of the frame body. The wording treats the frame body together with the mounting boss 70 joined to it as one cut element, which preserves the brief's existing statement that the boss is hatched like the body, and requires the cam ring to differ from it. FIG. 4 and FIG. 6 already carry the same rule, so all four sectioned sheets now state it identically.

**Rendered sheets.** A listing confirms `figures/` holds only the six Markdown briefs and `review/` only `previous-qa.md`; there is no image file and no figure-audit evidence file. Figure files are specifications and the sheets and evidence come from the image pipeline, so I created no images and altered no numeral definition, brief allocation or "shown in FIG. N" passage. The briefs place all 26 numerals with none unplaced and none on two parts: 100, 10, 12, 14, 16, 30, 40, 90 on FIG. 1; 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 34, 36 on FIG. 2; 18, 20, 30, 32, 34, 38, 40, 44 on FIG. 3; 22, 24, 36, 50, 52, 54, 56, 58 on FIG. 4; 18, 20, 70, 80 on FIG. 5; 10, 12, 18, 22, 24, 28 on FIG. 6.

Brief bodies stand at 2363, 2386, 2404, 2723, 1883 and 2722 characters, all within the limit, and the claims, detailed description, numeral table and drawing descriptions are unchanged and in step.

input.summary: Fixed the hatching gap in figures/FIG-3.md, whose rule now requires the frame body, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriage 30 with its follower 32, and the jaw pad 40 each to carry hatching at a slant different from every other cut element it touches or lies beside in the view, covering the follower inside the oblique slot 34 and the jaw pad hanging on the carriage. I applied the same rule to figures/FIG-5.md, where the segmented cam ring 20 lies in the groove of the frame body, wording it so that the frame body together with the mounting boss 70 joined to it counts as one cut element, which preserves that brief's existing statement that the boss is hatched like the body. FIG. 4 and FIG. 6 already carried the rule, so all four sectioned sheets now state it identically. The remaining finding is the empty drawing set: a listing confirms figures/ holds only the six Markdown briefs and review/ only previous-qa.md, with no image file and no figure-audit evidence file anywhere. Figure files are specifications and the sheets and evidence come from the image pipeline, so no image was created and no numeral definition, brief allocation or shown-in-FIG passage was altered; the briefs place all 26 numerals with none unplaced and none on two parts. Brief bodies stand at 2363, 2386, 2404, 2723, 1883 and 2722 characters, all inside the limit, and the claims, detailed description, numeral table and drawing descriptions are unchanged and synchronized.
reasoning: FIG. 3 was the sheet where identical hatching would do the most damage, because the follower sits inside the oblique slot with its faces against the slot sides and the jaw pad hangs directly on the carriage. If those pairs shared a slant the drawing would show one solid body where the text describes a follower driven along a slot and a pad free to pivot, which is the mechanism the claims recite. The pairwise rule fixes that without naming any slant, so no rendering value is invented.

I extended the same rule to FIG. 5 although the finding named only FIG. 3, because the reviewer's reason was that the drawing set is internally inconsistent on this point and FIG. 5 shows the cam ring lying in the groove of the frame body, the same contact FIG. 3 has. # FIG. 1

Plan view of the split pipe clamp closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

The pipe 90 is seen end on at the centre of the drawing area and appears as one circle, the area within it blank. An annular frame body surrounds it, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from the pipe 90 and by an outer circle. The ring-shaped space between the pipe 90 and that inner circle is open, crossed only by the jaw pads 40 and the inner ends of the jaw carriages 30.

Two radial joint lines, at the left and at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10, the lower the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, shown schematically as a small circle on that joint line between the inner circle and the outer circle, with a short block reaching to it from each frame end, the whole hinge 14 lying within the width of the frame body.

At the right joint is the latch 16, shown schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with a lever reaching radially outward from it, inclined toward the first frame half 10, the over-center attitude.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, at the top, the lower left and the lower right, the topmost on the first frame half 10 and the others on the second frame half 12. At each position the inner circle is interrupted by a radial opening and the jaw carriage 30 is shown schematically as a block reaching radially inward through that opening, its outer portion within the body and its inner end inside the inner circle.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30, its outer end just outside the outer circle and its inner end at the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the right, both on the same side of the line, giving the direction in which FIG. 3 is viewed. Each end carries the numeral 3 as the section designation, just outside that end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3; it is not a reference numeral.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer circle of the frame body at the upper left, away from the pipe 90.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the topmost carriage block.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the topmost carriage inner end.
- 90 pipe: target the interior of the central circle, inside the inner circle.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; the wedge 52, the latch housing 58, each cam ring segment and each frame body carry hatching at a slant different from that of every other cut element it touches or lies beside in the view; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the latch housing and its cavity, the interruption in the frame wall, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude and mounting of the latch handle 50, its action on the force-limiting spring stack 54, and that stack drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second such body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing the upper side of that band. Near the right end of that exposed side the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface, its left end high at the level of the exposed upper side and its right end low within the band, so the face descends from left to right, toward the parting line. Its right end stops short of that line, a short piece of the exposed upper side running on from it to the line.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward over the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity; its lower face descends from left to right at the same slant and rests on the ring drive face 36 along its length, so downward movement of the wedge 52 presses the left band toward the left.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot, so the stack lies between them.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening between the top and right walls, leaning past upright, the over-center position; it is a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which its position is read.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching of the right band.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

content.text:
The blocking cause is unchanged and I verified it directly: a workspace-wide search for `*.png`, `*.svg` and `*.json` returns nothing, so no sheet has been rendered and `review/figure-audit-evidence.json` does not exist. All four mechanical entries trace to that one absence, and the finding states that no specification text, claim, numeral definition or brief wording needs to change to cure it.

I made two small refinements to the briefs, both required by the standing drafting rules rather than by the finding, and neither touching the invention:

- **`figures/FIG-1.md`** no longer prescribes that the pipe 90 "appears as one circle." That was a face-linework control of the kind the instructions say to remove. It now reads as positive geometry: the pipe 90 is seen end on at the centre of the drawing area as a circle with its interior blank. The separation that matters is still carried positively by the next sentence, where the ring-shaped space between the pipe and the frame's inner circle is open and crossed only by the jaw pads 40 and the inner ends of the jaw carriages 30.
- **`figures/FIG-4.md`** now declares the outline of the latch handle 50 as schematic alongside its attitude and mounting, so the straight bar of even width is properly identified as a depiction convention rather than an asserted shape. The claims and description remain shape-neutral about the handle.

Everything else is untouched and verified in step: each brief's body numerals match its own list, no sheet lists more than eight numerals, the six lists place all 26 numerals of `draft/numerals.md` with none unplaced and none on two parts, the 3-3 designation is identical in FIG. 1, FIG. 3, the Brief Description and the detailed description, and the brief bodies measure 2347, 2386, 2404, 2732, 1883 and 2722 characters.

What closes this gate is rendering `figures/rendered-FIG-1.png` through `rendered-FIG-6.png` from these briefs and regenerating the audit evidence against the resulting image hashes. Figure files here are Markdown specifications and the pixels come from the image pipeline, so I did not create image or evidence files.

input.summary: The blocking defect is again the absent drawing set, and I confirmed it directly: a workspace-wide search for png, svg and json files returns nothing, so no sheet has been rendered and review/figure-audit-evidence.json does not exist. All four mechanical entries trace to that single absence, and the finding states that no specification text, claim, numeral definition or brief wording needs to change to cure it, so I left the certified text and the numeral allocations alone. I made two small brief refinements required by the standing drafting rules rather than by the finding, neither touching the invention: figures/FIG-1.md no longer prescribes that the pipe 90 appears as one circle, which was a face-linework control, and now states positively that the pipe 90 is seen end on at the centre of the drawing area as a circle with its interior blank, the separation from the frame's inner circle still being carried by the open ring-shaped space crossed only by the jaw pads 40 and the inner ends of the jaw carriages 30; and figures/FIG-4.md now declares the outline of the latch handle 50 schematic alongside its attitude and mounting, so the straight bar of even width reads as a depiction convention rather than an asserted shape. Everything else is verified in step: each brief's body numerals match its own list, no sheet lists more than eight numerals, the six lists place all 26 numerals with none unplaced and none on two parts, the 3-3 designation is identical in FIG. 1, FIG. 3, the Brief Description and the detailed description, and the brief bodies measure 2347, 2386, 2404, 2732, 1883 and 2722 characters. Rendering the six sheets from these briefs and regenerating the audit evidence is what closes the gate.
reasoning: I checked the cause myself rather than taking the report at face value: a recursive search for image and json files across the workspace returns nothing at all. That rules out a render that produced bad pixels and points to sheets never landing here, which is consistent with the numeral check reporting every numeral missing and with FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 being described as having stored sheets that are not on disk.

I did not fabricate image or evidence files. Figure specifications in this workspace are Markdown, the pipeline draws the geometry and places numerals, leaders and section annotation deterministically from them, and the audit evidence is bound to the resulting image hashes. A file written by hand would assert a verification that never happened.

The two edits I did make come from the standing instructions, not from the finding. Prescribing that the pipe appears as one circle is exactly the kind of one-stroke outline control the rules say to replace with positive geometry, and it is no longer needed: the open ring-shaped band between the pipe and the frame's inner circle, crossed only by the pads and carriage ends, is what keeps those two circles apart.

Declaring the latch handle outline schematic closes a smaller gap of the same kind. The disclosure gives a latch handle but no shape, so the straight bar of even width is a depiction convention; naming it as one in the brief keeps an undisclosed shape from reading as an embodiment while leaving the claims and description shape-neutral.

I deliberately left everything the review certified untouched, including the pairwise hatching rule now stated on all four sectioned sheets, the isolated-subassembly wording for FIG. 2 and every numeral target. Two turns of this gate have failed on the same physical cause, and editing certified text to look responsive would risk introducing a defect where none exists.

figures/FIG-4.md: the schematic list now covers the attitude, outline and mounting of the latch handle 50, so its straight bar of even width is declared a depiction convention
input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the draft contains no citation, so there is no reference to distinguish or mischaracterise. The Background states the problem conditionally, and each problem it states is answered by a feature recited in claim 1: cam ring segments recoupled by the act of closing the frame so one latch input reaches all three jaw carriages through a single coupled ring, follower and oblique slot pairs that convert that rotation into synchronized radial travel, and a force limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge that absorbs the operator's remaining handle travel instead of driving one jaw harder than the others. No claim or supporting passage changed this turn.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments drawn in the relative positions they occupy when coupled in the closed condition, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the positions and tilt of the three slots, and the position and length of the ring drive face 36.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike and all tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short straight flat cut into the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24, in the arc running downward from the right joint. Its upper end, the end nearer that joint, lies radially inside the outer boundary and stops below the joint, so a short piece of the circular outer boundary runs on from it to the joint. Its lower end, further from the joint, meets the circular outer boundary. Between the two ends the flat is one straight edge, so the material cut from the segment is deepest at the upper end and runs out to nothing at the lower end. Elsewhere both outer boundaries are circular.

content.text:
Both findings are fixed inside the figure briefs, with no change to the specification.

**Ring drive face form and depth.** `figures/FIG-2.md` now declares as schematic "the position, length, form and depth of the ring drive face 36," so the flat cut into the outer boundary and its depth gradient read as depiction choices rather than asserted structure. `figures/FIG-4.md` correspondingly declares "the length, form and slant of the ring drive face 36." The description remains as it was, saying only that the face lies at an inclination to the direction in which the wedge 52 advances.

**Wedge advance direction and lower-face slant.** `figures/FIG-4.md` now also declares as schematic "the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the slant of its lower face." The two sheets still show a consistent, renderable drive geometry, but nothing in them stands as an assertion about a direction the disclosure does not give. The description continues to say only that the wedge has an inclined face bearing on the ring drive face 36 and that latch movement advances it against that face.

The added declarations needed room in FIG. 4, so I removed only redundancy there: a trailing restatement that the spring stack lies between the handle and the wedge, which the same sentence already conveys by running it from the wedge up to the handle, and four short wordings condensed without losing a body, contact or direction. FIG. 4's brief is 2743 characters and FIG. 2's is 2399, both within the limit, and the claims, description, numeral table and drawing descriptions are untouched and in step.

input.summary: Both minor findings are fixed by extending the schematic declarations inside the figure briefs, with no change to the specification. figures/FIG-2.md now declares as schematic the position, length, form and depth of the ring drive face 36, so the flat cut into the ring's outer boundary and its depth gradient read as depiction choices rather than asserted structure, and figures/FIG-4.md declares the length, form and slant of the same face. figures/FIG-4.md also declares as schematic the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the slant of its lower face, so no direction of wedge travel stands as an invention assertion. The detailed description is unchanged and still says only that the ring drive face lies at an inclination to the direction in which the wedge advances and that the wedge has an inclined face advanced against that face. The added declarations needed room in FIG. 4, so I removed only redundancy there: a trailing restatement that the spring stack lies between the handle and the wedge, which the same sentence conveys by running the stack from the wedge up to the handle, plus four short condensations that drop no body, contact or direction. FIG. 4's brief is 2743 characters and FIG. 2's is 2399, both within the limit, and the claims, description, numeral table and drawing descriptions are untouched and synchronized.
reasoning: Both findings are about the same failure mode: a render-time geometric choice that carries technical substance because it fixes the rotation sense of the coupled ring, sitting outside the schematic declaration that would mark it as a depiction convention. The cure is to widen the declaration, not to change the geometry, because the sheets still need one internally consistent drive geometry to render at all.

I kept the drive geometry exactly as it stands. FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 agree on which segment carries the face, which end is deepest and which way the wedge presses, and that agreement is what earlier reviews verified. Removing the slant would have left the renderer free to draw a face that no longer converts wedge travel into the ring rotation the oblique slots need.

Nothing was added to the specification. The description already speaks only of an inclination to the direction of wedge advance and an inclined wedge face, which is the level of detail the disclosure supports, so the claims and description stay neutral while the briefs carry the depiction choices under an explicit schematic flag.

FIG. 4 had about twenty characters of headroom once both declarations went in, so I paid for them out of duplication. The clearest case was the clause saying the spring stack lies between the handle and the wedge: the same sentence already describes it rising from the wedge to the handle, and the disclosed relationship is stated in full in the detailed description and recited in claim 1.

I left the numeral targets, the hatching rule and every structural sentence alone. The review certified the source ledger, the numeral assignments and the cross-figure geometry, so the only edits this turn are the two declarations the findings named and the trimming needed to fit them.
